days.title: Listening to a child who stutters
days.teach: The Stuttering Foundation advises parents to slow their own speaking pace, keep natural eye contact, and give a child time. Don't finish their words or tell them to "slow down" or "start over." Listen to what a child says, not how they say it. A calm, unhurried home makes speech easier for everyone.
days.do: During one-on-one time, slow your own speech and wait.
days.ask: Did I interrupt or finish anyone's words today?
days.talk:
James asks every man to be quick to hear and slow to speak. For most fathers that verse is about anger. Today it is about something gentler, the pace of your listening.

When a child who stutters struggles to get a word out, everything in a father wants to help. Finish the sentence. Tell him to slow down. Tell him to take a breath and start over. It feels kind. But the Stuttering Foundation advises parents against every one of those.

Why is it so hard not to jump in? Because watching your child struggle is painful. A father is wired to fix things, and a stuck word looks like something to fix. There is also the hurry of family life. Someone is waiting, the car needs to leave, the other children are talking. Finishing the word feels like rescuing him. But to the child, it can feel like being taken over, and it tells him the struggle is something to get past quickly rather than something his father can sit with.

Here is what they recommend instead. Slow your own speaking pace. Keep natural eye contact. Give him time. Don't finish his words. Don't tell him to slow down or start over. Those instructions, however gentle, tell him that the way he talks is a problem you are watching.

Picture dinner. Your son starts to tell a story about recess and gets caught on a word. His sister jumps in, you finish the word for him, and the table moves on. He goes quiet for the rest of the meal. Now picture it again. He gets caught on the word. You keep your eyes on him, relaxed, and gently raise a hand toward his sister to say wait. He finds the word. He finishes the story. You laugh at the funny part and ask what happened next. He talks longer that night than he has in a week.

The most important shift is this. Listen to what he says, not how he says it. When he tells you about the game, or something he built, or something funny from school, respond to the story. Laugh at the funny part. Ask about the game. Let him feel that his ideas are what you care about.

Then look at the pace of your house. Mornings that run at full speed. Dinners where everyone talks over everyone else. A father who answers before the question is finished. A calm, unhurried home makes speech easier. When you slow down, you set the pace for everyone around you.

Some fathers wonder whether they should be doing more. If your child stutters, a speech therapist can be a real help, and these habits at home are not a replacement for that. They are what make the rest of his life easier, in the place he spends the most time. And with brothers and sisters, a simple family rule helps everyone. One person talks at a time, and nobody finishes anyone else's sentences.

Proverbs warns that answering before you have heard is folly. James says it more simply. Be quick to hear and slow to speak. For most fathers that is a spiritual discipline. With a child who stutters, it is also a practical gift. Every time you wait, you tell him there is room for his voice in this family.

Remember Moses. When God called him at the burning bush, Moses protested that he was slow of speech and slow of tongue. God did not take back the call. He sent Aaron to stand beside him, and Moses went on to lead his people. Scripture never treats Moses' speech as a reason he could not lead. It treats it as part of who he was when God chose him.

Your son is listening for the same message from you. Not that his speech does not matter, and not that you are pretending not to notice, but that it does not change how much you want to hear him. A father who waits calmly is telling his child that his voice belongs in this house exactly as it is. Few gifts will stay with him longer.

So during your time alone with your child today, pay attention to your own speed. Bring it down. Leave pauses. And when your child is working through a word, keep your eyes soft, stay with him, and wait for as long as it takes. Every child feels that difference.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is slow, patient listening. During your one on one time with each child, you will slow your own speech down and wait for them to finish every sentence.

This helps every child feel heard. For a child who stutters, it is a real gift, because a calm, unhurried listener makes speaking easier. If one of your children stutters, give this time to that child first.

Here is how to do it. First, slow your own pace. Speak a little more slowly than usual, with small pauses between sentences. Your child will tend to match your pace without being told to.

Second, keep natural eye contact. Look at your child the way you would during any easy conversation. Do not stare, and do not look away when a word gets stuck.

Third, wait. When your child is working on a word, stay quiet and relaxed. Do not finish the word, and do not say slow down, take a breath, or start over. Count silently in your head if it helps you stay patient.

Fourth, answer the story, not the speech. If your child tells you about a game, ask about the game. That sounds exciting. What happened next?

You can also leave a short pause after your child finishes before you reply. That one second tells them there is no rush.

A few things to avoid today. Interrupting. Asking several questions in a row. Answering before the question is done.

Tonight, notice how often you were tempted to jump in, and how it felt to wait instead.
days.fact: Proverbs chapter 18, verse 13 says that if one gives an answer before he hears, it is his folly and his shame. Proverbs ties wisdom to the ear before the mouth again and again. For a father, the verse is a plain warning against finishing another person's sentence, or answering a child before the child has finished speaking.

dailyVerse.text: There is a time to tear and a time to sew, a time to keep silence and a time to speak.

days.church: The Church teaches, in the Catechism paragraphs eighteen twenty-five and eighteen twenty-six, that charity is the love Saint Paul describes, a love that is patient and kind, that bears all things and endures all things. Patience is not only for big trials. It is also the quiet decision to wait while a child finds his words, so that he knows his voice is welcome.

days.title: Daughters and fairness
days.teach: Fairness and competence matter a lot in the middle years of childhood, and a daughter watches how you treat her brothers and sisters. Don't compare the kids. Praise each one for their own effort. Daughters learn from their fathers how a man treats the people he loves.
days.do: In one-on-one time, ask your daughter to teach you something she loves.
days.ask: Do I compare the kids out loud?
days.talk:
James tells every man to be quick to hear and slow to speak. A daughter in the middle years of childhood needs exactly that from her father, because she is listening closely to how you treat everyone in the house.

Somewhere in the middle years of childhood, a daughter starts keeping score. Fairness matters a lot at this age, and so does competence. She wants to be good at things, and she wants to know the rules are the same for everyone. That is why she watches how you treat her brothers and sisters. Every exception, every softer tone, every extra pass gets noted.

This makes comparison dangerous. Why can't you be more like your brother? He never complains about that. Even a passing comparison tells a child that your love is being measured against someone else. And it sets the two of them against each other in a contest neither one asked to enter.

Why do good fathers compare? Usually because it feels like motivation. If she sees her brother doing it right, maybe she will try harder. It is a shortcut, and it comes out fastest when we are tired. Fathers also tend to treat sons and daughters differently without noticing, sometimes softer, sometimes stricter, sometimes simply less curious about what she is doing. She notices even when you don't.

Picture dinner. Your son tells a long story about his game, and you ask question after question. Then your daughter says she finally landed the hard part of her piano piece, and you say, nice, and turn back to your plate. Nobody meant anything by it. But she heard it. Now picture it again. When she mentions the piano, you put your fork down and ask her which part was hard and how she finally got it. Her brother waits his turn. Both children leave the table feeling seen.

So don't compare the kids, out loud or in your tone. Praise each one for their own effort. Her work at practice, the way she handles a hard day, the recital or the race or the jump she was nervous about and went through with anyway. Those belong to her. They do not need a sibling as a measuring stick.

Some fathers will say that children are not the same, so they cannot be treated the same. That is true. Fair does not mean identical. An older child may stay up later, and a younger one may need more help. Fair means each child gets what he or she needs, and the reasons are explained calmly. A daughter can accept a different rule. What wounds her is a different level of interest.

Watch, too, for comparisons that sound like compliments. You're the easy one. At least you never give me trouble. A daughter who hears that may start to believe her place in the family depends on never needing anything. She may stop telling you when something is wrong. Praise what she does, not how much less trouble she is than someone else. Let her be good without having to be better than anyone.

There is something deeper here, too. Daughters learn from their fathers how a man treats the people he loves. She is watching how you speak to her mother, how you handle frustration, whether you listen when she talks. Without anyone saying it, she is learning what to expect from men. You are setting that standard every day.

At the end of the book of Job, after all his losses, Scripture takes the time to name his three daughters, and says their father gave them an inheritance along with their brothers. He saw each of them plainly and treated them as fully his own.

The Gospels show the same care. When Jairus came begging for his little daughter, Jesus went to his house. He took the girl by the hand and told her to rise, and she got up. Then he told them to give her something to eat. He did not only work a miracle. He thought about what a hungry little girl would need next.

So today, let her be the expert. In your time together, ask your daughter to teach you something she loves, whether it is a sport, music, riding, or a game. Then be a willing student. Ask real questions, and let her show you what she knows.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is letting your daughter be the expert. In your time alone with her, ask her to teach you something she knows and loves, then be a willing student.

This works because it shows her that you value her skill and her knowledge for its own sake, not in comparison to anyone else. It also gives her the experience of a man who listens to her and takes her seriously.

Here is how to do it. Choose something she cares about. A sport, an instrument, riding, drawing, a video game, a craft, or a subject she likes at school. Say something like, I don't really know how this works. Will you teach me? Then let her lead. Ask real questions. How did you learn that? What's the hardest part? What do you do when it goes wrong? Try it yourself if you can, and let her correct you without getting defensive.

For example. If she plays piano, ask her to show you a simple piece. If she plays soccer, ask her to teach you a move in the backyard. If she rides, ask her how she gets a nervous horse to settle.

When you finish, name what you saw. You explained that really clearly. You were patient with me.

Two cautions for today. Do not compare her to a brother or sister, even kindly. And do not take over the lesson. If you have no daughter, give this same time to each of your children.
days.fact: In Job chapter 42, verses 13 through 15, after Job's restoration, Scripture names his three daughters, Jemimah, Keziah, and Keren-happuch, while his seven sons go unnamed. It adds that their father gave them an inheritance along with their brothers. In Israel, daughters ordinarily inherited only when there were no sons, so Job's choice stands out as a father's deliberate honor.

dailyVerse.text: In all the land no women were as fair as the daughters of Job, and their father gave them an inheritance among their brothers.

days.church: The Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs twenty-two thirty-two and twenty-two thirty-three, teaches that family ties are important but not absolute, and that each child has his or her own vocation from God. Your daughter is not meant to be a copy of her brother. Praising her own effort, without comparison, honors the particular person God is calling her to be.

days.title: United front
days.teach: Kids find any gap between parents and push on it. Parents being inconsistent with each other is one of the strongest drivers of behavior problems. Disagree in private and present one answer. If your wife has asked for no yelling, honoring that in front of the kids builds trust with everyone in the house.
days.do: Ten-minute check-in with your wife after the family meeting. Ask what she's noticed.
days.ask: Did I undercut her this week, even with a look?
days.talk:
This week James has asked you to be quick to hear and slow to speak. That verse is not only about your children. It is about your wife, and today it is about the two of you together.

Kids are excellent engineers. They find any gap between their parents and push on it. Dad said no, so I'll ask Mom. Give them two answers and they will pick the one they like, and over time they learn to set you against each other.

This matters more than most parents realize. Parents being inconsistent with each other is one of the strongest drivers of behavior problems in children. Not the occasional disagreement. The steady pattern of one parent undoing the other.

Why do loving parents drift apart on rules? You were raised in different homes, with different ideas of what is normal. One of you is often home more and carries more of the daily load. And there is a quiet pattern many couples fall into. If one parent gets harsh, the other softens to make up for it. Then the first gets harsher to make up for the softness. Neither one is wrong to care. But the gap keeps widening, and the children live inside it.

Picture bedtime. You told your son no more screens tonight. Ten minutes later he finds his mother in the kitchen and asks her for one more show. She doesn't know you already said no, and says sure. You walk in, see the screen, and say, I already told him no, right in front of him. Now the evening is about the two of you. Picture it again. When he asks, she says, what did Dad say? Or she says yes, and you let it stand for tonight, and the two of you sort it out later behind a closed door. Either way, he learns that asking the other parent does not change the answer.

The answer is not that you and your wife must agree on everything. You won't. The answer is to disagree in private and present one answer. If she makes a call you would have made differently, back her in the moment and talk about it later, behind a closed door. And watch the small signals. A sigh or a look across the table can undercut her as surely as words.

But what if you truly think she is wrong? Unless someone is unsafe, wait. Most calls are not worth a public correction. Bring it up later, calmly, as a question rather than a verdict. You may find she saw something you missed. And if you both slip into the same old habits, focus on your own part. You can only keep your half of the front.

There is a special weight to this for you right now. If your wife has asked you to stop yelling, she has named it, and you are working on it. Every time you honor that in front of the kids, you are doing more than keeping a promise to her. You are building trust with everyone in the house at once. The kids see a father who listens to their mother. Your wife sees a husband who takes her seriously. And you become a more trustworthy man in your own house.

The book of Proverbs opens by telling a son to hear his father's instruction and not to forsake his mother's teaching. Two voices, one direction. That is the united front Scripture has in mind.

Luke gives us a picture of it in the Holy Family. When the boy Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem, Mary and Joseph searched for him together for three days. When they found him in the temple, Mary said, your father and I have been looking for you. Not I. Your father and I. Even in their worry, they spoke as one.

The Church teaches that in marriage a man and a woman become one flesh. That oneness is not only something that happened at the altar. It is lived out in ordinary evenings, in who answers a child's question and how. Every time you back your wife in front of the children, you are showing them what that unity looks like with its sleeves rolled up.

So after the family meeting today, find a few quiet minutes alone with your wife. Not to report on how well you have done, but to ask her what she has seen this week. Then listen to her answer.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is a ten minute check-in with your wife after the family meeting. You ask what she has noticed over the last two weeks, and you listen.

A check-in is a short, private conversation between parents about how the plan is going. It keeps you a united front, because problems get talked through behind a closed door instead of fought out in front of the children.

Here is how to do it. After the meeting, once the kids are busy or in bed, find a quiet spot. Phones away. Then ask open questions and let her talk. What have you noticed in me these last two weeks? Have I undercut you, even with a look? Where do the kids seem to be playing us against each other? What's one thing you'd like me to keep doing?

Your job is to listen, not to report on how well you have done. If she names something hard, do not explain or defend it. Say, thank you for telling me. Then ask, what would help?

Before you finish, agree on one thing together. It might be a rule you both need to enforce the same way, a time of day that needs more help, or a phrase you will both use. For example. When either of us says no, the other one backs it. Or, if the kids ask one of us after the other has answered, we say, what did your mom say?

End by thanking her. Then keep this check-in going every week.
days.fact: Proverbs chapter 1, verse 8 tells a son to hear his father's instruction and not to forsake his mother's teaching. The Hebrew word for the mother's teaching is torah, the same word used for God's law. Proverbs chapter 6, verse 20 repeats the pairing. From its opening lines, the book presents father and mother as one teaching voice.

dailyVerse.text: The two shall become one flesh, so they are no longer two but one. What God has joined together, let no man separate.

days.church: The Church teaches, in the Catechism paragraphs sixteen forty-one and sixteen forty-two, that husband and wife receive a proper grace of the sacrament of marriage, to help one another and to raise their children. You and your wife are not two separate authorities. You share one vocation, and the grace to live it is given to you together, including in how you answer a child.

days.focus: Ask once, up close, as a statement. Wait 10 seconds. Calm consequence. Correct in private, never in front of siblings or friends.
days.verse: A soft answer turns away wrath; a harsh word stirs up anger.
days.title: ABC
days.teach: Alan Kazdin teaches it as A-B-C: Antecedent, Behavior, Consequence. Most parents focus on consequences. The bigger lever is the antecedent, meaning how you set up the request: timing, tone, how close you are, and how clear it is. Fix the setup and you'll need far fewer consequences.
days.do: Before one request today, set it up well: get close, make eye contact, be specific.
days.ask: What came right before today's worst moment?
days.talk:
This week the verse comes from Proverbs. A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger. For two weeks you have worked on your own heart. Now you turn to your words, starting with what happens before you even speak.

Alan Kazdin teaches parents a simple framework he calls A, B, C. Antecedent, behavior, consequence. The antecedent is what comes before. The behavior is what the child does. The consequence is what follows.

Most parents put almost all their energy into the consequence. What do I do after he refuses? How do I respond to the eye roll? But the bigger lever is the antecedent, meaning how you set up the request. The setup shapes what happens far more than most of us realize.

Why do we focus on the consequence? Because that is where the drama is. The refusal is loud, and the consequence feels like action. The setup is invisible. It happens in a second, from wherever we happen to be standing, while our mind is on something else. Nobody thinks of a shouted request from the next room as a choice. But it is one, and it often decides the next ten minutes.

Think about what goes into it. Timing. Asking for homework the moment a child walks in the door is different from asking after a snack. Tone. A tired, irritated voice predicts a fight. How close you are. Calling from the kitchen to a child upstairs almost guarantees being ignored. And how clear it is. Clean up a bit is fog. Put your shoes and backpack by the door is something a child can actually do.

Picture an afternoon. Your son is on the couch with a tablet. From the kitchen, while stirring a pot, you call out, time for homework. Nothing. You call louder. He says, in a minute. Five minutes later you are standing over him, angry, and the homework starts in a bad mood. Now picture it set up well. You give him a snack first. Then you walk over, sit down next to him, wait for him to look up, and say calmly, in five minutes the tablet goes on the charger and you start your spelling at the table. The same child, the same afternoon, and a very different outcome.

Surgeons know this well. Good operations are won before the first incision. Positioning, prep, the plan, the right instruments on the tray. A surgeon who skips the setup spends the case fighting complications. A father who skips the setup spends the evening handing out consequences. Fix the setup and you will need far fewer of them.

Some fathers object. Shouldn't children obey no matter how I ask? In an ideal world, perhaps. But you are the adult, with the patience and the planning a child is still growing into. A good setup is not coddling. It is leading well. You are not lowering the bar. You are giving your child a fair chance to clear it.

And what if you set it up perfectly and he still refuses? Sometimes he will. The setup does not guarantee obedience. It lowers the odds of a fight, and it makes the fights that do happen smaller. When a refusal comes after a good setup, you will also know it is a real refusal and not a misunderstanding. That makes the next step, the calm consequence, much easier to give fairly.

This week's verse from Proverbs says a soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger. Notice that the verse is about what comes first. The softness or the harshness at the start shapes everything that follows. That is antecedent wisdom, written long before anyone gave it a name.

Scripture has a living example. In the first book of Samuel, David was riding out in anger with his men to destroy the household of Nabal, who had insulted him. Nabal's wife Abigail went out to meet him. She brought food for his men, and she spoke to David humbly and wisely. David's anger cooled, and he thanked God that she had kept him from bloodshed. She changed the outcome by changing how the moment began.

So before one request today, stop and set it up on purpose. Walk over. Get down to eye level. Look at the child. Say exactly what you want, in words they can act on. Then watch what happens.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is setting up one request on purpose, before you make it.

Alan Kazdin's A, B, C stands for antecedent, behavior, and consequence. The antecedent is everything that comes just before your request. Today you work on that part, because a well set up request often needs no consequence at all.

Pick one request you make most days, the one that usually goes badly. Shoes on. Screens off. Start homework. Come to dinner. Then set it up in four steps.

First, timing. Choose a moment when the child can actually listen. Not mid sentence, not the second they walk in hungry.

Second, get close. Walk over to the child. Do not call from another room.

Third, get their attention. Get down to eye level, say their name, and wait until they look at you. A light hand on the shoulder helps.

Fourth, be specific and calm. Say exactly what you want in plain words, at normal volume.

Here is what it sounds like. Instead of shouting from the kitchen, get ready for bed, walk to the couch, kneel down, say your child's name, and wait for eye contact. Then say, teeth brushed and pajamas on now. Instead of clean up a bit, say, books on the shelf, please. Instead of come on, we're late, say, shoes on and stand by the door.

Then watch what happens. Tonight, think back to the hardest moment of the day and ask what came right before it. That is your antecedent, and tomorrow you can set it up better.
days.fact: Proverbs chapter 22, verse 6 tells parents to train up a child in the way he should go. The Hebrew verb for train, chanak, is also used for dedicating a new house in Deuteronomy chapter 20, verse 5, and for dedicating the Temple in First Kings chapter 8, verse 63. It shares its root with Hanukkah. Training a child means setting him up from the start.

dailyVerse.text: David said to Abigail, Blessed be the Lord who sent you to meet me today, and blessed be your good sense, which kept me from bloodshed.

days.church: The Code of Canon Law, canon eleven thirty-six, says parents have the most grave duty and the primary right to care for the whole education of their children, physical, social, cultural, moral and religious. The Catechism, paragraph twenty-two twenty-three, adds that teaching virtue in the home requires sound judgment. Setting up a request with care is part of that duty, done wisely.

days.title: The effective instruction
days.teach: Say it as a statement, not a question. Give one instruction at a time. Be specific. Say what to do ("walk") instead of what not to do ("don't run"). Get close, and use a calm, neutral tone. "Can you maybe clean up?" invites a no. "Legos in the bin now" does not.
days.do: Turn every question-request into a statement today.
days.ask: How many times did I repeat an instruction?
days.talk:
This week's proverb tells us that a soft answer turns away wrath. Yesterday you worked on setting up a request. Today you work on the words themselves.

How you phrase an instruction decides a great deal about whether it gets followed. Here is the difference. Can you maybe clean up invites a no. Legos in the bin now does not.

Questions sound polite, and that is why we use them. But a question offers the child a choice, and if you did not mean to offer one, you have just set up a fight. So say it as a statement, not a question.

Why do good fathers drift into questions and hints? Some of us grew up with fathers who barked orders, and we promised ourselves we would never sound like that. So we soften everything until it turns vague. Others are simply unclear in their own heads. We know we are frustrated, but we have not yet decided exactly what we want done. A fuzzy request is often a sign of a fuzzy plan.

And there is the habit of tone. When a father is frustrated, his instructions tend to come out wrapped in commentary. How many times do I have to tell you? Why is this still on the floor? Those sentences are not instructions at all. They are complaints shaped like questions, and a child has no idea how to answer them. Strip the commentary away and only the instruction is left. That is usually all that was needed.

Give one instruction at a time. Go upstairs, brush your teeth, put on pajamas, and lay out your clothes for tomorrow is four instructions, and most kids will hold onto one. Give the first, wait for it, then give the next.

Be specific. Clean your room is a hope. Clothes in the hamper is a task.

Say what to do instead of what not to do. Don't run puts the word run in the child's head. Walk tells them exactly what you want.

And get close. Use a calm, neutral tone. Instructions shouted across the house are easy to ignore and easy to resent. An instruction given at arm's length, at normal volume, carries more weight than any yell.

Picture a Saturday morning. The living room floor is covered in toys. You say, from the doorway, hey guys, can we maybe clean this up a little? Someone says, in a minute. Twenty minutes later nothing has moved, and you are louder. Now picture it again. You walk in, crouch next to your daughter, and say, blocks in the bin, please. She starts. When the blocks are in, you say, thank you, now the books on the shelf. One task, then the next, at normal volume, and the floor is clear before anyone has raised a voice.

Notice that please was still there. A statement is not rude. You can say please and thank you and still give a clear instruction. What you leave off is the question mark that turns a direction into a vote. And if your child still does not follow it, that is not a sign the method failed. It means you need the next pieces, the calm wait and the follow through, which are coming in the days ahead.

There is something steadying in this. You do not need to be louder. You need to be clearer. Think of a surgeon asking for an instrument. Short, specific, calm, and expected to be followed. Nobody in the room hears it as rude.

This week's verse from Proverbs reminds you that a soft answer turns away wrath. Soft here does not mean vague. It means calm. A clear instruction in a quiet voice is about the gentlest form authority can take.

At the wedding in Cana, when the wine ran out, Mary said to the servants, do whatever he tells you. Then Jesus gave them two short instructions. Fill the jars with water. Now draw some out and take it to the steward. They did, and the water had become wine. Clear words, calmly given, and the servants simply followed.

So listen to yourself today. Each time a request starts to come out with a question mark on the end, catch it, and say it again as a plain, kind sentence. You may be surprised how often it happens.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is turning every question request into a statement.

An effective instruction is a clear, calm statement of exactly what you want done. It works because it does not offer a choice you did not mean to offer, and it tells the child exactly what success looks like.

Listen for requests that end in a question. Can you put your shoes on? Would you like to clean up? How about we start homework? Okay? Each of those invites a no. Today, catch them and turn them into statements.

Use five rules. Say it as a statement. Give one instruction at a time. Be specific. Say what to do, not what not to do. And get close, with a calm, neutral voice.

Here are some swaps. Instead of, can you maybe clean up, say, Legos in the bin now. Instead of, could you get ready for bed, say, pajamas on, please. Instead of, don't run, say, walk. Instead of, clean your room, say, clothes in the hamper. Instead of, go upstairs, brush your teeth, put on pajamas, and pick a book, give only the first step, then the next one once it is done.

A statement can still be kind. Please and thank you belong in it. What changes is the question mark.

If you catch yourself asking, simply say it again as a statement. Let me say that better. Shoes on now, please. Then keep a rough count of how many times you had to repeat yourself today.
days.fact: In Ephesians chapter 6, verse 4, Paul pairs two Greek words. Paideia, built on the word for a child, means training or upbringing. Nouthesia joins the words for mind and to place, so it means putting something in mind, a word of instruction or warning. Paul's picture of fatherly discipline is clear words placed in a child's mind, not force.

dailyVerse.text: Jesus said to the servants, Fill the jars with water. And they filled them up to the brim.

days.church: The Code of Canon Law, canon seven seventy-four, paragraph two, teaches that parents, above all others, are obliged to form their children in faith and in Christian living, by word and by example. Your words are part of how you form them. Clear, calm instructions given once are a small daily example of how a Christian man speaks to those in his care.

days.title: Warnings before transitions
days.teach: Sudden transitions set off defiance, especially in kids who struggle with executive function. A five-minute and a one-minute warning let the brain shift gears. Then give the instruction once. A visible timer helps, because then the clock ends the activity, not you. No third warning, no negotiation.
days.do: Give a five-minute warning before screens go off.
days.ask: Which transitions in our day are the roughest?
days.talk:
A soft answer turns away wrath, says this week's proverb, but a harsh word stirs up anger. Some of the harshest words in a house are not insults at all. They are sudden commands that land with no warning. Today you learn to soften the edges of the day.

Some of the hardest moments in any house happen at the seams of the day. Screens off. Time to leave for school. Bath now. Bed now. These transitions are where a calm evening can turn in thirty seconds.

There is a reason for that. Sudden transitions set off defiance, especially in kids who struggle with executive function. Shifting from one activity to another is real mental work. The brain has to let go of what it was doing, take in something new, and line up the steps to get there. For a child who finds that hard, an abrupt command feels like being pulled out of the water mid stroke.

Why do fathers keep springing transitions without warning? Because we carry the schedule in our heads and forget that our children do not. You have known all afternoon that dinner is at six. To your son, absorbed in his game, dinner arrives out of nowhere. There is also simple busyness. The warning slips our mind until the moment has already come, and then we are in a hurry, and the hurry makes our voice sharp.

Warnings let the brain shift gears. A five minute warning lets the child know an ending is coming. A one minute warning tells them to start wrapping up. Then you give the instruction once. Not a third warning. Not a negotiation. One clear instruction, because the warnings already did the preparing.

Picture the screen going off before dinner. In one version, you walk into the living room and say, turn it off, dinner's ready. Your son says he is in the middle of a level. You say now. He says just one minute. You reach for the controller, and dinner starts with a slammed door. In the other version, you stop by the couch earlier and say, five minutes, then it goes off for dinner. Later, one minute, finish what you're doing. Then, time's up, it goes off now. He groans, but he expected it, and he turns it off.

Make the warnings concrete. Five minutes left, and then the tablet goes on the charger. One minute, finish your level. Then, time is up, tablet on the charger. A timer the child can see helps even more, because then the clock ends the game, not you.

Some fathers worry the warnings will become a new thing to bargain over. Five more minutes, please? That is why you give no third warning and no negotiation. The warnings are a gift, not an opening. Others say that real life does not give warnings. Sometimes it doesn't. In an emergency, you give the instruction and expect it followed. But most transitions are not emergencies, and the warning trains a skill your child will use for the rest of his life, the skill of seeing an ending coming and getting ready for it.

Think of how God led Saint Joseph in Matthew's Gospel. When the angel sent the family into Egypt, he told Joseph to stay there until he was told. In time the word came that it was safe to return. Joseph was not left guessing about the next move. Even heaven gave the Holy Family notice before a big change.

If you have a child who struggles more than most with transitions, add one more piece. Tell him what comes after. Five minutes, then the tablet goes off, and then we'll walk the dog together. A child finds it easier to let go of something when he can see what he is moving toward. An ending with nothing on the other side feels like a loss. An ending with a next step feels like a change.

And notice how Joseph answered that notice. Each time the angel spoke, Matthew tells us, Joseph rose and did as he was told, without delay and without argument. Clear warning and calm obedience went together. That is the rhythm you are trying to build in your house, one evening at a time.

So start with the screen transition today. Before you ask anyone to turn anything off, give the warning ahead of time, then a last one, and then one calm instruction. Notice how differently the evening ends.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is a transition warning before screens go off.

A transition warning is a heads up that one activity is about to end and another is about to begin. It works because it gives a child's brain time to let go of what it is doing, so the end does not come as a shock.

Here is how to do it. Choose the moment. The screen transition is a good place to start, because it is often the hardest. Then follow three steps.

First, give a five minute warning. Go to the child, get close, and say it clearly. Five minutes left, and then the tablet goes on the charger. Wait until the child acknowledges it, even with a nod.

Second, give a one minute warning. One minute. Finish your level or your episode scene.

Third, give one instruction, once. Time is up. Tablet on the charger. Then wait calmly. If it does not happen, follow through with the consequence you and your wife already agreed on.

A visual timer helps a great deal. Use a kitchen timer, a phone timer the child can see, or a clock with a colored wedge that shrinks. When the timer goes off, the timer ends the game, not you.

You can use the same pattern for other hard transitions. Leaving the park. Bath time. Leaving a friend's house. Turning off the light at bedtime.

Avoid giving a third warning or negotiating for more time once the timer ends. Tonight, notice which transitions in your day are the roughest, and plan warnings for those next.
days.fact: In Matthew chapter 2, verse 13, the angel tells Joseph to take the child and his mother to Egypt and to stay there until he is told. Then in verses 19 and 20, after Herod dies, the angel returns and tells him it is safe to go back. Joseph is led through each transition with a word before the move.

dailyVerse.text: An angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream and said, Rise, take the child and his mother, flee into Egypt, and stay there until I tell you.

days.church: The Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs five thirty-one and five thirty-two, reflects on the hidden life of Jesus at Nazareth, where he was obedient to Mary and to Joseph. The Son of God lived inside the ordinary rhythm of a family's day. A house where changes are announced and then calmly carried out shares a little of that holy order.

days.title: The 10-second wait
days.teach: After an instruction, wait silently. Kids need time to process. When you repeat yourself, you train them to wait for the third, loudest request. Ask once, wait, then follow through. Stay close and calm during the silence. If nothing happens, follow through without a speech.
days.do: Ask once, then count to ten silently. Every time.
days.ask: Did silence work better than repeating myself?
days.talk:
This week's proverb warns that a harsh word stirs up anger. Very often in a family, the harsh word is not the first request. It is the third. Today is about the quiet seconds that keep you from ever reaching the third.

After you give an instruction, the next ten seconds matter more than you might think. Most fathers fill them. We repeat ourselves, add a reminder, raise the volume a notch. Silence feels like being ignored, so we rush to break it.

Why is the silence so hard to bear? Partly because we are in a hurry, and every second feels like lost time. Partly because a child who does not move instantly looks like he is defying us, and something in a father rises to meet a challenge. And partly because silence leaves us exposed. While we wait, we do not know what will happen, and saying something again feels like doing something. But often, doing something is exactly what gets in the way.

But kids need time to process. A child in the middle of something has to hear you, stop what they are doing, understand what you asked, and get their body moving. That takes a few seconds. If you speak again before they have finished, you interrupt the very thing you asked for.

Worse, repeating yourself trains them. If the first request is always followed by a second and a third, they learn the first one is optional. The real request comes later, and louder. You end up training them to wait for the third, loudest request, which is exactly the version of you that you are trying to retire.

Picture the hallway before school. You say, coat on, please. Your daughter is still looking at a book. Two seconds later you say, coat, now. Then, did you hear me? By the time she reaches for the coat, your voice has an edge, and she is sulking. Now picture it again. You say, coat on, please, and you stand there, quiet and close, hands at your sides. One second, three, six. She closes the book, sighs a little, and reaches for the coat. You say, thank you. Nobody raised a voice, and the morning stayed intact.

So ask once, then wait. Silently. Stand there, calm and close. No sighing, no tapping your foot, no raised eyebrows that say what are you waiting for. Just presence and patience. Very often, before the silence runs out, the child starts to move.

If the silence passes and nothing has happened, follow through. That is the other half. The wait only works when the child knows that after it, something real happens, calmly and without a speech.

Some fathers find ten seconds feels like forever the first few times. That is normal. Count slowly in your head, and give it a week before you judge it. Others worry that a stubborn child will simply wait them out. Then you follow through, and the child learns that waiting you out does not work. The silence is not a hope. It is a pause before action.

And what you do during the wait matters as much as the wait itself. Stay where you are. Do not drift back to your phone or walk away to start something else, because then the request quietly expires. Your calm presence says, I meant this, and I am right here. Children can feel the difference between a father who is waiting and a father who has already moved on.

James tells us to be slow to speak. A few seconds of silence after a request is about as practical as that verse gets. It looks like nothing. It is actually a form of strength, the strength of a man who trusts his word enough to say it once.

Saint John tells of a moment when the scribes and Pharisees brought a woman to Jesus and pressed him for an answer. He did not rush. He bent down and wrote with his finger on the ground. When they kept pressing, he stood and spoke a single sentence, and then he bent down and wrote again. His silence gave everyone room to think, and one by one they went away.

So make a rule for yourself today. Every time you give an instruction, close your mouth and let the count run in your head. See whether the silence does more than repeating ever did.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is the ten second wait. Every time you give an instruction, you will say it once and then count to ten silently before you say anything else.

The ten second wait is a short, quiet pause after a request. It works because children need a few seconds to stop what they are doing, understand you, and start moving. When you repeat yourself, you teach them that the first request does not count.

Here is how to do it. Give a clear instruction, up close, in a calm voice. Shoes on, please. Then close your mouth and count slowly in your head to ten. Stay close. Keep your face relaxed. No sighing, no foot tapping, no raised eyebrows, no reminders.

Very often the child starts to move before you reach ten. When that happens, notice it and praise it. Thank you for coming right away.

If you reach ten and nothing has happened, follow through calmly. That might mean giving a short warning of the consequence once. If your shoes aren't on by the time I count to five, you'll lose ten minutes of screen time tonight. Or it might mean gently guiding a younger child through the task. Then do exactly what you said, with no speech.

Here is a scene. You say, backpack by the door. Your son keeps building. You stay where you are and count. At seven, he sets down the block and goes. You say, thanks, buddy.

Tonight, ask yourself whether silence worked better than repeating.
days.fact: In James chapter 3, verses 1 through 3, James warns that not many should become teachers, since teachers will be judged more strictly, and then he turns to the tongue. He compares it to the bit in a horse's mouth, small but able to steer the whole animal. A father, his children's first teacher, steers much with a little restraint.

dailyVerse.text: The man who holds back his words has knowledge, and the man of understanding keeps a cool spirit.

days.church: The Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs twenty-two fifteen to twenty-two seventeen, teaches that children owe their parents respect and obedience. Obedience is something a child gives, and he needs room to give it. A calm, silent wait after a clear request offers him that room, and it lets his obedience be his own response rather than something squeezed out by a raised voice.

days.title: Calm consequences
days.teach: Consequences work because they're certain and immediate, not because they're big. Deliver them flatly, without sarcasm. Then it's over: no lecture, no grudge, no bringing it up at dinner. A small consequence every time beats a big one now and then. When it is finished, return to warmth right away.
days.do: Use one pre-agreed consequence today, calmly, with no lecture.
days.ask: Did I add a speech to the consequence?
days.talk:
A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger. Today the proverb meets the hardest moment of all, the moment after a child has crossed a line.

When a child pushes past a limit, there is a pull to make the consequence big. No screens for a week. No friends over for a month. The bigger it is, the more it feels like justice. But consequences work because they are certain and immediate, not because they are big.

Why do we reach for big ones? Because the size of the consequence tends to match the size of our anger, not the size of the offense. And often we have let things slide for days, so when we finally act, we are acting on the whole week at once. There is also a fear underneath. If the consequence is small, will it matter? Will the child even care? So we go bigger, and then we cannot hold it, and the child learns that our consequences are loud but do not last.

A small consequence that happens every time, right away, teaches far more than a huge one that happens now and then, long after the fact, when you finally snap. Kids learn from patterns. If rude talk at dinner means leaving the table for a few minutes, then it has to mean that every time, today and tomorrow and when Grandma is visiting. Certainty is what makes it fair.

Then there is the delivery. Deliver it flatly, without sarcasm. Not, well, I guess somebody wants to lose their screens. Just the fact. You kept playing after I asked, so the tablet goes on the charger for the night. Calm voice, plain words, no drama. Sarcasm turns a consequence into an insult.

Picture dinner. Your son says something rude to his sister. In one version, you lose patience, tell him he has lost his phone for a week, and then spend ten minutes explaining why he deserves it. He stews for the rest of the meal, and by Wednesday you have quietly given the phone back. In the other version, you say calmly, that was rude, go sit on the stairs for a few minutes. He goes. He comes back. You pass him the potatoes and ask about his day as if nothing happened. The consequence was small, it was done, and the meal went on.

And then it is over. No lecture, no grudge, no bringing it up at dinner. The consequence is the whole response. When you add a speech, the child stops thinking about what they did and starts thinking about how unfair you are. When you hold a grudge, you are punishing twice. When you raise it again at dinner, you shame them in front of everyone.

Some fathers say small consequences will never work on their child. They may not work the first time. They work through repetition, over weeks, because the child slowly learns that the limit is real every time. And if you and your wife disagree about consequences, settle it ahead of time, in private, so that neither of you has to invent one in the heat of the moment.

Proverbs says the Lord reproves the one he loves, as a father reproves the son in whom he delights. The correction comes out of delight, and it does not cancel the delight. When it is finished, the child should feel your warmth again right away.

This is how God treats us. The psalm says that as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us. When a sin has been confessed and forgiven, he does not bring it back up the next day. A father who lets a finished consequence stay finished is giving his children a small taste of that mercy.

It helps to have a short list ready before you need it. A few minutes away from the table. The tablet on the charger for the evening. An earlier bedtime by a little. Small, calm, and easy to carry out. When the list already exists, you do not have to invent anything while you are angry, and you are far less likely to reach for something too big to keep.

So today, when a limit is crossed, reach for one of the consequences you have already agreed on. Say it calmly, follow through, and then let it be finished.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is one calm consequence, taken from the list you and your wife already agreed on, with no lecture attached.

A consequences menu is a short list of small, fair consequences that both parents agree on ahead of time, so no one invents a punishment while angry. It works because children learn from certainty and speed, not size.

If you have not made your menu yet, take five minutes with your wife to make one today. Keep each item small and easy to carry out right away. For example. Thirty minutes off screens tonight. Leaving the table for five minutes. An earlier bedtime by fifteen minutes. An extra chore, like emptying the dishwasher. Losing a toy that was thrown, until tomorrow.

When a limit is crossed today, follow three steps. First, state what happened in one short sentence. You kept playing after I asked. Second, give the consequence flatly, in a calm voice. So the tablet goes on the charger for the night. Third, stop. That is the whole response.

Avoid three things. No sarcasm, such as, I guess somebody wants to lose their screens. No speech about respect or responsibility. And no bringing it up again at dinner, or holding a grudge.

Once the consequence is done, return to warmth quickly. Ask about their day. Offer a hug. Let the child feel that the matter is closed.

Tonight, ask yourself honestly whether you added a speech, and if you did, notice what it cost.
days.fact: Proverbs chapter 3, verses 11 and 12 say not to despise the Lord's discipline, because the Lord reproves the one he loves, as a father reproves the son in whom he delights. The Letter to the Hebrews quotes this passage when it speaks about discipline. In both places, correction flows from a father's delight, not from his anger.

dailyVerse.text: As far as the east is from the west, so far has the Lord removed our sins from us.

days.church: The Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs twenty-three oh two and twenty-three oh three, warns against anger that becomes a desire for revenge, and it recalls the Lord's words about everyone who is angry with his brother. A consequence is meant to teach, never to get even. Small, calm and finished, it corrects the behavior without wounding the child or the relationship.

days.title: Choices within limits
days.teach: Kids heading into adolescence need some control. Two acceptable options give them that without giving up the limit: "Homework at the kitchen table or your desk?" "Shower before or after dinner?" They pick the how, and you hold the what.
days.do: Offer three either-or choices today.
days.ask: Where am I fighting over control I could share?
days.talk:
A soft answer turns away wrath. One of the softest answers a father can give is a choice. Today you learn how to share control without giving up the limit.

Kids heading into adolescence need some control. That is not rebellion. It is growth. A child who is growing up needs practice making decisions, and if every decision is made for him, he will start fighting over the ones that are yours to make.

Why does this catch good fathers off guard? Because when our children were small, we decided nearly everything, and it worked. What to wear, what to eat, when to sleep. Then, almost without warning, a child who used to go along starts pushing back on everything. It can feel like disrespect, and many fathers respond by tightening their grip. But a growing child is supposed to want more say in his own life. The question is whether he gets it in small, safe ways from you, or has to fight you for it.

The answer is not to give up the limit. It is to share the parts you can share. Two acceptable options give them that control without giving up the limit. Homework at the kitchen table or your desk? Shower before or after dinner? Do you want to set the table or clear it?

Look at what is happening in those questions. The homework still gets done. The shower still happens. The table still gets set. They pick the how, and you hold the what. The child gets a real choice and the dignity that comes with it, and you get the outcome you needed without a battle.

Picture the evening shower. In one version, you say, go take your shower. Your son says, I'll do it later. You say, now. He says, why now? Ten minutes later you are arguing about hygiene and fairness, and he still has not moved. In the other version, you say, shower before dinner or right after? He thinks for a second and says, after. After dinner you say, it's after dinner. He goes. The shower happened, and nobody had to win.

A few things make it work. Both options have to be ones you can truly live with. If one of them is a trap, kids sense it right away. Keep it to two, because three or four options start to feel like a negotiation. And once they choose, honor it, even if you would have picked the other one.

What if the child refuses to choose, or invents a third option? Stay calm and say, those are the two choices. If you don't pick, I'll pick for you. Then wait a few seconds. If he still does not choose, you choose, kindly, and move on. The limit holds either way. And if a child keeps choosing in a way that does not work, you can take that option off the list next time and explain why.

Choices also work beautifully before trouble starts. A child who has been given a say in small things all day comes to the big things with less to prove. If he chose his seat at dinner, picked the order of his chores, and decided which book to read at bedtime, he has had plenty of practice being trusted. There is less fight left in him, because there is less he needs to win.

Think of the father in the parable of the prodigal son. When his younger son asked for his share, the father gave it. He did not control every step his sons took. He let them be persons, even at real cost, and he kept watching the road. Your stakes are much smaller, but the principle holds. Respect grows where a child is trusted with real decisions.

From the very beginning, God shared real decisions with us. In Genesis, he brought the animals to the man to see what he would call them, and whatever the man called each one, that was its name. God gave the man one clear command in the garden, and within it, he let the man choose a great deal. That is the pattern of good authority, firm limits and real freedom inside them.

So look for the fights you keep having over small things, the where and the when, and turn them into choices. Find a few moments today to hand each child a simple choice between two, and let them own what they pick.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is offering three either or choices.

A choice within limits gives a child two options you are truly happy with. It works because the child gets real control over how something happens, while you keep the final say over what happens.

Here is how to do it. Look for the small battles you keep having, the ones about where, when, or how. Then turn each one into two choices. Keep it to two, because more starts to feel like bargaining. Make sure you are fine with either answer. Then honor whatever the child picks.

For example. Homework at the kitchen table or at your desk? Shower before dinner or after? Do you want to set the table or clear it? Do you want to wear the blue jacket or the green one? Do you want to walk to the car or hop like a rabbit? Do you want to brush your teeth first or put on pajamas first?

Notice what is not a choice. Homework still happens. The shower still happens. The jacket still goes on.

If your child refuses both options or offers a third, stay calm and repeat once. You can pick this or this. If they still do not choose, say, then I'll choose for you, and do so calmly.

Spread your three choices across the day, ideally one in the morning, one after school, and one in the evening. Tonight, notice where you were fighting over control you could have shared.
days.fact: In Luke chapter 15, verse 12, when the younger son asks for his share, the father divides his property between his sons. The Greek word Luke uses for property is bios, which also means life or livelihood. The father of the parable gives his sons real freedom, even when it costs him, and keeps watching the road for the son who leaves.

dailyVerse.text: The Lord God brought the animals to the man to see what he would call them, and whatever the man called each one, that was its name.

days.church: The Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraph twenty-two twenty-two, teaches that parents must regard their children as children of God and respect them as human persons. A growing child is a person learning to use his freedom well. Giving him real choices within firm limits respects that freedom, while you keep the responsibility that belongs to you as his father.

days.focus: Ask once, up close, as a statement. Wait 10 seconds. Calm consequence. Correct in private, never in front of siblings or friends.
days.verse: A soft answer turns away wrath; a harsh word stirs up anger.
days.title: Routines do the reminding
days.teach: A posted routine reminds the kids so you don't have to nag. When the morning list is on the wall, you point to it instead of repeating yourself. Kids follow routines they helped build more readily. Keep each list short, and post it where the routine actually happens.
days.do: At the family meeting, draft the morning, homework, and bedtime routines with the kids.
days.ask: Which routine causes the most fighting right now?
days.talk:
A soft answer turns away wrath, says this week's proverb. Some of the softest answers in a house are not spoken at all. They hang on the wall, and they say the same thing every morning without ever raising their voice.

Think about how much of your talking in a day is reminding. Brush your teeth. Did you pack your lunch? Where is your homework folder? Shoes. Shoes. Shoes. Most of the nagging in a family is not about new rules. It is about the same few steps, every day, said over and over.

Why does nagging take over a house? Because the steps of a routine live in the parents' heads, not the children's. A child lives in the present moment. He is not thinking about the bus. He is thinking about the toy in his hand. So the father becomes the household checklist, and a checklist that talks gets tuned out. Each reminder wears a little thinner than the last, until by the fifth one the voice is sharp and everyone is tense, over steps that happen every single day.

A posted routine reminds the kids so you don't have to nag. When the morning list is on the wall, you do not repeat yourself. You point to it. What's next on the list? The list becomes the authority on the small things, and you get to stay calm and friendly. The friction moves off you and onto a piece of paper, and a piece of paper is very hard to argue with.

Picture a school morning without a list. You are making lunches and calling out reminders over your shoulder. Teeth. Shoes. Did you get your folder? Your son keeps drifting back to the couch, and with each reminder your voice gets a little tighter, until you are both out the door upset. Now picture the same morning with the list on the wall by the door. He wanders toward the couch. You say, what's next on your list? He looks, sees shoes, and puts them on. You did not have to name a single step yourself.

There is one more key. Kids follow routines they helped build more readily. A routine handed down from above feels like a set of orders. A routine they helped write feels like theirs. Let them suggest the order. Let them decide whether teeth come before or after pajamas. Let one of them draw a small picture next to each step.

Some fathers have tried a chart before, and it lasted two weeks. That is normal. A list fades from view the way anything on a wall does. Keep each list short, and post it where the routine actually happens, the bathroom mirror for teeth, the door for the morning. Look at it together at the weekly family meeting and change what is not working. A routine is a living thing, not a single project. And if a child ignores the list, you do not start nagging again. You point, and you wait.

For a child who cannot read yet, use pictures. A toothbrush, a shirt, a backpack, a pair of shoes. Let him draw them himself if he likes. For an older child, the list can be shorter and plainer, or kept on a card in his room. The form matters less than the principle. The steps live somewhere outside your voice, so your voice can be saved for warmth.

The Law of Moses understood this long ago. In the book of Deuteronomy, right after the great command to love the Lord with all your heart, the people were told to write those words on the doorposts of their houses and on their gates. They did not trust memory alone. They put what mattered where everyone would see it, every time they came in or went out.

The Church has always known the power of a steady daily order. Saint Benedict wrote a rule for his monks that shaped their whole day around set hours of prayer, work, and rest. And the Church still prays the Liturgy of the Hours, morning and evening, every day of the year. A good routine is not a cage. It frees the mind for what matters most.

So at the family meeting today, make this a shared project. Bring paper and markers. Ask for their ideas, write down what they say, and work through the three parts of the day that cause the most friction. Then decide together where each list will hang.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is drafting your family's routines with your children at the family meeting. Morning, homework, and bedtime.

A routines chart is a short, posted list of the steps for one part of the day, in order. It works because the list does the reminding, so you point to it instead of nagging. Children also follow a routine more readily when they helped build it.

Here is how to do it. Bring paper and markers to the meeting. Explain the idea in a sentence or two. We keep reminding you about the same things every day. Let's make lists so we don't have to.

Take one routine at a time. Ask, what has to happen before we leave for school? Write down every answer. Then put the steps in order together. Let the children decide small things, like whether teeth come before or after getting dressed.

Keep each list short, around five to seven steps. For example, a morning list might read. Get dressed. Make your bed. Eat breakfast. Brush teeth. Shoes and backpack by the door. A bedtime list might read. Bath. Pajamas. Teeth. Pick a book. Prayer. Lights out.

For younger children, draw a small picture next to each step, or let them draw it.

Then decide together where each list will hang, like the bathroom mirror, the fridge, or the back of the front door. Tomorrow, when a step is forgotten, point and ask, what's next on your list?
days.fact: Deuteronomy chapter 6, verses 8 and 9 tell Israel to bind God's words on their hands, set them between their eyes, and write them on the doorposts of their houses and on their gates. Jewish families still fix a small case called a mezuzah to the doorpost. The command put what mattered most where the whole household would see it every day.

dailyVerse.text: You shall write these words of the Lord on the doorposts of your house and on your gates.

days.church: The Church teaches, in the Catechism paragraph twenty-two twenty-four, that the home is the natural place to begin learning solidarity and shared responsibility, and paragraph twenty-six eighty-five calls the Christian family the first place of education in prayer. A routine the whole family builds together, with a prayer at the end of the bedtime list, teaches both lessons at once.

days.focus: Write morning, homework, and bedtime routines with the kids. Post them. All Saints, Nov 1.
days.verse: Fathers, do not embitter your children, lest they lose heart.
days.title: Make executive function visible
days.teach: Russell Barkley's main point is that kids with executive function weakness can't hold time and steps in their heads. So put them outside the head: checklists, timers, visual clocks. Some of what looks like laziness or defiance is really a missing skill.
days.do: Give your child a visual checklist for one routine.
days.ask: Am I calling a skill gap defiance?
days.talk:
This week the verse comes from Paul's letter to the Colossians. Fathers, do not embitter your children, lest they lose heart. It is a short warning, and it asks you to think about what a child feels when he keeps failing at the same thing.

Russell Barkley's main point is a simple one. Kids with executive function weakness can't hold time and steps in their heads. For most adults, getting ready in the morning runs on an inner list and an inner clock. We barely notice them. For a child who struggles with executive function, the inner list fades, and the clock is hard to feel at all.

Why is this so easy to miss? Because you cannot see a missing skill. You can see a boy sitting in the hallway with one shoe on, and it looks like a choice. Worse, he managed the whole routine just fine last Saturday, so it seems he can do it when he wants to. But skills like these are uneven. They hold up on an easy, rested morning and fall apart on a rushed, noisy one. To a busy father, that unevenness looks exactly like not trying.

So you put them outside the head. Checklists, timers, visual clocks. A card on the bathroom mirror with each step of the morning. A timer on the counter that shows the minutes running down as a shrinking colored wedge. A list taped inside his folder for what needs to come home. You are not doing the work for him. You are giving him a tool that does what his brain is still learning to do.

This matters because some of what looks like laziness or defiance is really a missing skill. When a boy stands in the hallway with one shoe on, it is easy to assume he isn't trying. Often the next step has simply slipped away and he cannot find it. Yelling at a missing skill does not build the skill. It only builds shame.

Picture a homework night. You tell your son to finish his assignment, and an hour later he has written his name and nothing else. You lose patience and tell him he is wasting everyone's time. Now picture it again. You sit down and help him break the assignment into three small parts. You write them on a sticky note. You set a timer he can see for the first part. When it rings, he checks it off and takes a short break. He finishes, and he is proud of it.

Notice what changed. The assignment did not get easier, and your son did not suddenly start caring more. What changed is that the steps and the time were put where he could see them. And you went from standing over him to sitting beside him. That shift in where you sit matters as much as the sticky note. It tells him that the two of you are working on the problem together, rather than you working on him.

Paul warns fathers not to embitter their children, lest they lose heart. A child who keeps failing at something he cannot yet do, and keeps getting blamed for it, will lose heart. A child given the right tool starts to succeed, and success gives heart back.

Think of the checklists in the operating room. They do not exist because surgeons are lazy. They exist because even skilled people drop steps under pressure. Nobody is insulted by them.

Some fathers worry that this is a crutch. Will he need a list forever? Look at your own life. Most adults run on calendars, alarms, and reminders, and no one thinks less of them for it. As the skill grows, the tools can shrink. And if you suspect your child struggles with these skills more than most, it is worth talking with his doctor or his school. Knowing what you are dealing with helps everyone.

Scripture has a picture of this. In the book of Exodus, while Israel fought below, Moses stood on the hill with his hands raised. As long as his hands stayed up, Israel prevailed. But his arms grew tired, so Aaron and Hur sat him on a stone and held up his hands, one on each side, until sunset. Nobody called Moses weak. They gave him what he needed to finish.

So choose one routine that keeps going sideways for your child. Build a simple list your child can see, and let your child be the one who checks things off.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is building a visual checklist for one routine that keeps going wrong.

Executive function is the brain's set of planning skills, like keeping steps in order, keeping track of time, and starting a task without being reminded. Some children are slower to develop these skills. A visual checklist puts those steps outside the head, where the child can see them, so the child can succeed without you hovering.

Here is how to do it. Choose one routine that regularly falls apart. Getting out the door. Packing the school bag. Getting ready for bed. Starting homework.

Then build the list with your child. Keep each step small and concrete. Not, get ready, but, shirt, pants, socks, shoes. Use pictures for younger children. Put it exactly where the routine happens, such as on the bathroom mirror, inside the front door, or taped inside a folder.

Add a way to check things off. A dry erase marker on a laminated sheet, sticky notes to move from one side to the other, or a magnet that slides down the list.

Pair it with a timer the child can see. A clock with a shrinking colored wedge, or a kitchen timer set for twenty minutes, makes time something a child can watch.

When your child gets stuck, point to the list instead of repeating yourself. What's next on your list?

And praise each checkmark. You did the whole list by yourself today.
days.fact: In Colossians chapter 3, verse 21, Paul tells fathers not to provoke their children, lest they become discouraged. The Greek verb he uses for losing heart, athumeo, appears nowhere else in the New Testament. Its root, thumos, refers to the spirit or inner passion. Paul's single use of the word warns fathers that harsh handling can drain the spirit out of a child.

dailyVerse.text: When Moses' hands grew weary, Aaron and Hur held them up, one on each side, so his hands stayed steady until the sun went down.

days.church: The Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraph twenty-two twenty-one, teaches that the role of parents in education is so important that it can hardly be replaced. Paragraph twenty-two twenty-eight adds that parents show their love through care and attention in raising their children. Noticing what a child truly cannot yet do, and building him a tool for it, is exactly that kind of care.

days.focus: Write morning, homework, and bedtime routines with the kids. Post them. All Saints, Nov 1.
days.verse: Fathers, do not embitter your children, lest they lose heart.
days.title: Kids do well if they can
days.teach: Ross Greene's premise: when a child can't meet an expectation, it's usually a lagging skill or an unsolved problem, not a lack of wanting to. That one idea moves you from opponent to coach. The question changes from "How do I make him?" to "What's getting in the way?"
days.do: After one blowup, ask yourself what skill was missing.
days.ask: Which expectation keeps failing, and why?
days.talk:
Paul tells fathers not to embitter their children, lest they lose heart. One of the surest ways to discourage a child is to believe he is failing on purpose when he is actually stuck. Today's idea can change that belief.

Ross Greene has a premise that changes how you see your children. Kids do well if they can. When a child can't meet an expectation, it is usually because of a lagging skill or an unsolved problem, not a lack of wanting to.

Most of us were raised on the opposite idea. Kids do well if they want to. So when a child fails, we assume he did not care enough, and our job is to make him care more. Louder voices. Bigger consequences. That approach turns you into an opponent. You stand on one side of the problem, and your child stands on the other.

Why do good fathers hold onto that older idea? Because it feels simpler. If the problem is will, then the solution is pressure, and pressure is something we know how to apply. It also matches what we have seen. He did his homework without a fight on Monday, so why not Thursday? But a child who can do something sometimes may not be able to do it every time, especially when he is tired, worried, or facing something new. Doing well once does not mean the skill is solid.

Greene's one idea moves you from opponent to coach. The question changes from how do I make him, to what's getting in the way. Maybe the homework fight is really about not knowing how to start a big assignment. Maybe the morning meltdown is about a shirt that feels wrong and no words to say so. Maybe the struggle to leave practice or the barn is about not being ready to stop something she loves. Once you see the obstacle, you can work on it together.

Picture a weeknight. Your son has melted down over his reading log for the third night in a row. You could take away his screen time again. Instead, the next afternoon, when nothing is at stake, you sit down with him and say, I've noticed the reading log has been really hard lately. What's up? He shrugs. Then he tells you he can never think of what to write in the summary box, and he feels stupid. Now you know what you are actually dealing with. You come up with a plan together, and the next night goes differently.

A good surgeon thinks this way about a complication. He does not blame the patient for bleeding. He finds the source and deals with it. That same calm curiosity works at home.

Some fathers worry that this excuses bad behavior. It does not. The expectation stays exactly where it was. The reading log still gets done. What changes is that you stop trying to force it through with pressure and start working on what is blocking it. And if you try this and your child has no idea what is getting in the way, that is normal too. Be patient, ask again another day, and offer your own guesses gently.

Timing matters here. Do not try to find the problem in the middle of the meltdown. A child who is upset cannot think clearly about what went wrong, any more than you can when you are flooded. Wait for a calm hour, when nothing is due and nobody is in trouble. Sit side by side if you can, in the car or on a walk. Children often talk more freely when they are not being looked at directly.

Think again of the father in Luke's parable. When his older son stood outside the feast, angry and refusing to come in, the father did not send word that he had better get inside. He went out to him. He came looking for whatever was in the way.

Our Lord asked questions like this. When blind Bartimaeus cried out to him on the road from Jericho, Jesus stopped and asked him, what do you want me to do for you? The answer may have seemed obvious. But Jesus asked anyway, and he listened. He let the man name his own need.

So after the next blowup today, once things are quiet, do the coach's work. Ask yourself honestly what skill was missing, or what problem has never been solved. That answer is where tomorrow's progress starts.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is asking what skill was missing. After one blowup today, once everyone is calm, you will stop and ask yourself what got in the way.

Ross Greene teaches that children do well if they can. When a child keeps failing at something, there is usually a lagging skill or an unsolved problem behind it, not a lack of wanting to. Asking about the skill turns you from an opponent into a coach.

Here is how to do it. First, get through the blowup calmly, using your exit line if you need it. Second, once things have settled, take five minutes alone. Third, answer three questions honestly. What exactly was expected of my child in that moment? What happened instead? What skill or problem might explain the gap?

Some common lagging skills. Shifting from one activity to another. Handling disappointment. Putting feelings into words. Getting started on a hard task. Keeping track of time. Tolerating noise, crowds, or uncomfortable clothes.

Here are a few examples. The homework fight may really be about not knowing how to start a big assignment. The morning meltdown may be about a scratchy shirt and no words to say so. The refusal to leave practice may be about not knowing how to stop something enjoyable. The fight at bedtime may be about being afraid of the dark.

Write your answer down in a sentence or two. Do not try to solve it yet. Just name it. Tonight, ask which expectation keeps failing in your house, and why.
