days.title: Children copy what you do
days.teach: Kids learn more from what they watch than from what they're told. Narrate your own calming: "I'm frustrated. I'm going to take a breath before I answer." You're teaching the skill out loud.
days.do: Narrate your own calming once today.
days.ask: What am I modeling when I'm stressed?
days.talk:
This week's psalm says that as a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has compassion on those who fear Him. Children first learn what compassion and self control look like by watching their father.

Kids learn more from what they watch than from what they are told. You can explain calm a hundred times. They will learn what calm actually looks like by watching what you do when the dishwasher breaks, when the car won't start, when a call comes in at dinner.

That is sobering, but it is also an opportunity. Most of the time, a child sees only the outside of a father's stress. A tight face. A slammed drawer. Or, on good days, nothing at all, because you handled it quietly inside. Either way, they don't see the skill. They see the result, or the explosion.

Why do so many fathers hide the inside? Because most of us were taught that a man handles things privately. Admitting frustration out loud feels like losing ground, especially in front of your children. So we swallow it, and sometimes it stays swallowed, and sometimes it leaks out sideways in a sharp word or a slammed door. Neither one teaches a child anything useful about what to do with a hard feeling.

So narrate it. Say out loud what is going on inside you and what you are doing about it. I'm frustrated. I'm going to take a breath before I answer. Then actually take the breath, where they can see it. It may feel awkward. It may even feel like weakness, admitting frustration to your kids. It isn't. You are teaching the skill out loud, in real time, with real stakes.

Picture a school morning. You are already running late, and a full glass of milk goes over the edge of the table. In one version of the morning, you let out a loud sigh, throw a towel at the mess, and ask why nobody in this house can be careful. Your children learn that when things go wrong, the right response is to get loud.

In the other version, you stop. You say, Okay. I'm frustrated, because we're late and now this. I'm going to take a breath. They watch you do it. Then you say, Alright, I'm calmer. Let's grab a towel. The milk gets cleaned up just the same. But your children just learned something no lecture could have taught them. Weeks later, you may hear your daughter, frustrated with a puzzle, say under her breath that she is going to take a breath. That is the moment you will know it landed.

Children don't need a lecture on self control after the fact. They need to see a grown man feel something hard and handle it, step by step, right in front of them. Then, the next time they are flooded, they have words they have actually heard someone use.

Won't it frighten a child to hear Dad say he is angry? Not if the narration ends in calm. What frightens children is anger with no words and no end. Anger that is named, handled, and finished is reassuring. And what if you are already too far gone to narrate anything? Then use your exit line and step away. When you come back, narrate it afterward. I was getting too angry, so I took a minute. That counts too.

Psalm one hundred three describes the Lord as merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love. Slow to anger describes what God does, not only what He feels. Your children will learn what slow to anger means by watching it in their own kitchen.

On the night before He died, Jesus knelt and washed His disciples' feet. When He finished, He told them, I have given you an example, that you also should do as I have done to you. Our Lord did not only explain humility. He showed it, with a towel in His hands, and then He told them what it meant. That is the pattern for a father. Show it, and then name it.

Ask yourself what you are modeling when the pressure is on. Then, sometime today when frustration rises, let your kids hear you name it, and watch you calm it.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is narrating your own calming, once, out loud, where your kids can hear. Most of the time children see only the result of a father's stress, either the explosion or nothing at all. Narrating lets them see the skill itself, step by step, so they have words to use when they are upset.

Here is how to do it. Wait for an ordinary frustration. The dishwasher breaks, the traffic stops, someone spills a full glass of milk, a work call comes at a bad time. When you feel the frustration rise, do four things out loud.

First, name the feeling. I'm frustrated. Second, say what you will do. I'm going to take a breath before I answer. Third, actually do it, slowly and visibly, so they can see your shoulders rise and fall. Fourth, name the result and the next step. Okay, I'm calmer now. Let's get a towel and clean this up.

More examples. I'm really annoyed that we're late. I'm going to count to ten before I say anything. Or. That email made me angry. I'm going to walk around the yard once before I decide what to do.

If the frustration is about something a child did, keep the narration about yourself, not about them. Say I'm feeling angry, not you made me angry. Then deal with the problem calmly.

It may feel awkward the first time. That is fine. You are teaching your children self control in real time, the way they learn best, by watching you.
days.fact: In John chapter five, verses nineteen and twenty, Jesus says the Son can do nothing on His own, but only what He sees the Father doing. Whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise, because the Father loves the Son and shows Him all that He Himself is doing. Jesus describes His own sonship as watching and imitating a loving Father who shows his work openly.

dailyVerse.text: I have given you an example, so that you also should do just as I have done for you.

days.church: The Church teaches, in canon seven seventy-four, section two, of the Code of Canon Law, that parents above all others are obliged to form their children in faith and Christian living, by word and by example. Children absorb example first. When your child watches you name your frustration, take a breath, and answer calmly, you are forming him in self-control.

days.title: Warm and firm
days.teach: Diana Baumrind's research described three styles. Authoritarian is high control, low warmth. Permissive is high warmth, low structure. Authoritative is high on both and consistently has the best outcomes. Respect comes from warmth plus consistency, not fear.
days.do: Notice where you slide authoritarian and where you slide permissive.
days.ask: Which way do I drift when I'm tired?
days.talk:
There is a line in this week's psalm that holds together two things many fathers think are opposites. A father's compassion, and a child's reverence. Researchers studying ordinary families found the same pairing.

Diana Baumrind's research described three parenting styles. Once you see them clearly, you will start to notice them in yourself.

Authoritarian parenting is high control and low warmth. Rules, orders, consequences, and not much tenderness behind them. Permissive parenting is the reverse. High warmth and low structure. Plenty of affection, very few limits.

The third style is authoritative. It is high on both. Warm and firm at the same time. Clear expectations, enforced consistently, by a parent who is obviously on the child's side. Of the three, this is the style that consistently has the best outcomes.

Here is the key. Respect comes from warmth plus consistency, not from fear. Fear can get you obedience in the moment, while you are standing there. Respect is what is left when you are at work and nobody is checking.

Most fathers don't live in one style. We drift. When we are rested and things are going well, we can hold warmth and firmness together. When we are tired, we slide. Some men slide toward authoritarian, getting short and controlling and barking orders. Others slide toward permissive, letting things go because they don't have the energy for one more fight. Knowing which way you lean is half the work.

Why do we slide at all? Because warmth and firmness both cost energy. Firmness takes the energy to follow through on what you said. Warmth takes the energy to stay gentle when you are irritated. When the tank runs low at the end of a long day, a tired man drops one of them, almost always without noticing. And most of us drop the same one every time.

Picture a homework battle on a weeknight. Your son is tired, the worksheet is long, and he says he can't do it. The authoritarian version of you says he will sit there until it is finished and you don't want to hear another word. The permissive version of you says fine, skip it, you'll write the teacher a note. The authoritative version sits down next to him and says, I know you're tired, and this is a lot. It still has to get done. I'll do the first problem with you, and then you take it from there. Same father. Same worksheet. Three very different evenings. Only one of them ends with homework finished and a boy who still feels like his father is on his side.

Some fathers worry that warmth will make them look soft, and the kids will stop taking them seriously. The opposite is usually true. A limit held by a warm father is easier to accept, because the child is not also fighting for the relationship. Others suspect that authoritative is just a nicer word for permissive. It isn't. In an authoritative home, the limit holds every time. What changes is the tone it is held in. A warm no and a cold no are both still no. Only one of them leaves the child feeling that his father is still with him.

This week's psalm holds both together. As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has compassion on those who fear Him. Compassion and reverence in the same breath. God is not soft, and He is not harsh. He is tender and He is firm, and He never stops being either one. That is the father you are trying to imitate.

You can see it in the Gospel of Mark. A rich young man ran up to Jesus and asked what he must do to inherit eternal life. Mark says that Jesus, looking upon him, loved him. And then, in that same love, He told the young man the hardest thing he had ever heard. Sell what you have, give to the poor, and come follow me. The man went away sorrowful, and Jesus let him go. He did not lower the bar, and He did not stop loving. Warm and firm, at the same moment.

So pay attention today. Notice the moments you tighten into control, and the moments you let something slide because you are worn out. Don't fix anything yet. Just learn your drift.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is learning your drift. You will simply notice when you slide away from warm and firm, and which way you slide.

A quick reminder of the three styles. Authoritarian means high control and low warmth. Orders, threats, and a sharp tone, with little tenderness behind them. Permissive means high warmth and low structure. Lots of affection, but limits that fade whenever enforcing them feels like too much work. Authoritative means high on both. Clear expectations, enforced calmly every time, by a father who is obviously on his child's side.

Here is how to do it. Go through your day as usual, but keep a quiet tally, on your phone or a scrap of paper, with two columns. Mark the first column each time you slide toward control. For example. Barking an order instead of asking. Threatening something you won't follow through on. Cutting off a child who is trying to explain. Mark the second column each time you slide toward letting it go. For example. Ignoring a broken rule because you are tired. Giving in after the third time a child asks. Doing a child's chore yourself to avoid the fight.

Do not try to fix anything today. Just notice and mark. Pay special attention to the late afternoon and evening, when most fathers are most tired.

Tonight, look at the two columns. Finish this sentence and write it down. When I'm tired, I tend to drift toward. That one line will guide the next few weeks.
days.fact: In Psalm one hundred three, verse thirteen, the Hebrew verb for a father's compassion is racham. It is closely related to rechem, the Hebrew word for womb. The tender, protective love the psalm ascribes to a father is described with language rooted in a mother's body. The same verse pairs that tenderness with the fear of the Lord, warmth and reverence held together.

dailyVerse.text: Jesus looked at him and loved him, and said, You lack one thing. Go, sell what you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me.

days.church: The Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraph twenty-two fourteen, teaches that divine fatherhood is the source of human fatherhood. A father learns what he is meant to be by looking at God, who is both tender and firm with His children. Warmth without limits and limits without warmth both fall short of Him. Hold the two together, and your fathering reflects its source.

days.focus: Advent began Nov 29. Keep the system boring and predictable. Add an Advent family prayer at dinner.
days.verse: As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has compassion on those who fear Him.
days.title: Sibling fights
days.teach: Don't referee every squabble. Stay out of minor ones, step in for safety, separate them and let them calm down, then solve it later. Praise them when they cooperate. Taking sides fuels the rivalry.
days.do: Let one minor squabble resolve without you.
days.ask: Am I the referee they're performing for?
days.talk:
This week's psalm speaks of a father's compassion on his children. Children, more than one. A father with several children has to hold compassion for all of them at once, and that is never harder than in the middle of a fight between them.

If you have more than one child, you have a full time job as a referee, if you want it. Don't take it.

Most sibling squabbles are minor. Who got the bigger piece. Who touched whose stuff. Who looked at whom. If you step into every one of them, you teach your kids two things. That they can't settle anything without you. And that the fastest way to get Dad's attention is to fight in front of him. Ask yourself honestly whether they are performing for the referee. Sometimes a fight that starts the moment you walk into the room is not about the toy at all. It is about you.

Why do good fathers keep stepping in? Because the noise wears on us, and stepping in feels like the fastest way to end it. Because men tend to have a strong sense of fairness, and an unfair split of anything sets it off. And because a crying child pulls at a father's heart. All of that is understandable. But every time you take the case, the courtroom stays open for business.

So stay out of the minor ones. Let them work it out, even if the solution is clumsy and loud. Step in when someone's safety is at stake. When you do step in, don't hold court on the spot. Separate them, let them both calm down, and solve it later, when nobody's heart is pounding.

Picture the back seat of the car. She's touching me. He's on my side. In one version, you turn around and demand to know who started it. Both talk at once. You decide the older one is to blame, the younger one smirks, and the war picks up again at the next red light. In the other version, you keep your eyes on the road and say, Sounds like you two have a problem. I bet you can work it out. There is some grumbling. A minute later they are arguing about something else, or laughing at the same song.

Whatever you do, don't take sides in the heat of it. Even when you are fairly sure who started it, taking sides fuels the rivalry. The child you rule against feels the sting and resents the one you sided with, and the fight just moves underground.

Scripture shows how deep that wound can go. Jacob loved Joseph more than any of his other sons, and he made him a special coat. When the brothers saw that their father loved Joseph more than all of them, Genesis says, they hated him and could not speak peaceably to him. A father's favor, plainly shown, set brother against brother for years.

What if one child really does seem to start it every time? Then you are looking at a pattern, not a squabble, and it deserves real attention, and patterns get solved at a calm time, one on one, the way you have been solving recurring fights. And what if your wife jumps in every time you hold back? Talk it over tonight, and agree on which fights the two of you will let run.

Then do the part most fathers forget. Watch for the moments when they cooperate. Building something together, laughing at the same joke, one helping the other with a chore. Praise them for it, specifically. Make cooperation the thing that earns your attention. A father who notices only the fights will get more fights. A father who notices the kindness will see more of it. Children go where the attention is.

Once a man in a crowd asked Jesus to tell his brother to divide the family inheritance with him. Jesus answered by asking who had appointed Him judge or arbitrator over them. He would not be drawn into a quarrel between brothers on demand. Instead He spoke to what was going on in the heart.

So today, when a small squabble starts, stay out of it. Let it run its course without you, and see what they do. You may be surprised how capable they are.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is letting one minor squabble between your children resolve without you. The goal is to stop being the referee, so that fighting no longer earns your attention and your kids get practice settling small things themselves.

First, know the difference. A minor squabble is about who sat where, who touched what, who got more, or who looked at whom. It is loud and annoying, but nobody is getting hurt. A safety situation is hitting, shoving, throwing things, or one child clearly overpowering another. Those you step into right away.

Here is how to do it. When a minor squabble starts, ask yourself one question. Is anyone in danger? If not, stay out. Keep doing what you were doing, or leave the room. If a child runs to you to report, hand it back calmly. For example. Sounds like you two have a problem. I bet you can work it out. Or. I trust you two to figure that out.

If it does turn unsafe, separate them without taking sides. For example. You go to the couch, you go to the kitchen. We will talk when everyone is calm. Solve it later, together, once nobody's heart is pounding.

Then watch for cooperation and use labeled praise, which means praise that names the exact behavior you saw. For example. You two figured out how to share the controller all by yourselves. That was great teamwork. Make cooperation the thing that gets your attention.

If you have only one child, apply this to a squabble with a friend or cousin.
days.fact: Psalm one hundred thirty-three opens by saying how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell together in unity. It is one of the Songs of Ascents, traditionally linked with pilgrims going up to Jerusalem. It compares that unity to precious oil running down Aaron's beard and to the dew of Mount Hermon. Peace among siblings is treated as a blessing, not a given.

dailyVerse.text: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God.

days.church: The Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs seventeen sixteen and seventeen seventeen, presents the Beatitudes, among them blessed are the meek and blessed are the peacemakers. Peace between brothers and sisters does not come from a father ruling on every quarrel. It grows when children practice settling small things themselves, and when their father notices and praises the moments they choose peace.

days.focus: Advent began Nov 29. Keep the system boring and predictable. Add an Advent family prayer at dinner.
days.verse: As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has compassion on those who fear Him.
days.title: Make the truth safe
days.teach: Kids lie to avoid punishment. Victoria Talwar's research found that children in a harshly punitive school lied more readily than those in a non-punitive one. Make telling the truth safer than hiding: telling the truth always lightens the consequence.
days.do: Tell the kids: telling the truth always makes it better here.
days.ask: Do my kids lie to me out of fear?
days.talk:
This week's psalm says that the Lord, like a father, has compassion on His children. Today we look at what a child does when he is not sure his father will be compassionate. He hides.

Kids lie to avoid punishment. That is the plain reason behind most lies a child tells. Not bad character. Fear.

Victoria Talwar's research found that children in a harshly punitive school lied more readily than children in a non punitive one. Think about what that means. The harsher the consequences, the stronger the pull to hide. A child does the math very quickly. If telling the truth brings the same punishment as getting caught, or worse, then hiding is the better bet.

So change the math. Make telling the truth safer than hiding. In this house, telling the truth always lightens the consequence. Always. If the window is broken, there is still a consequence for the window. But the child who comes to you and says I did it gets a lighter one than the child you had to catch.

Why do good fathers end up punishing honesty without meaning to? Because the truth usually arrives at the worst moment. A child admits something, and it is the first you have heard of it. The surprise and the frustration land all at once, on the only person standing in front of you, and that person is the one who just told you the truth.

Picture your son walking up to you holding the television remote in two pieces. In one version, you erupt. You what? How many times have I told you? He stands there and takes it. And he learns something. Next time, the pieces go into the bottom of the trash, under the paper towels. In the other version, you take a breath. You say, Thank you for telling me. That took courage. Let's see if it can be fixed. If it can't, he helps pay for a new one, a little at a time. The consequence is real. But he walks away knowing that coming to you was the right call.

You have to keep that promise every time, especially when you are angry. The first time a child confesses and you explode anyway, the deal is broken, and they will remember. Take the breath. Thank them for telling you. Then deal with the problem calmly.

Being believed matters here too. A child who tells the truth and is not believed learns that honesty doesn't work. When your child tells you something, start from trust unless you have a real reason not to.

Some fathers worry that kids will take advantage, and confess everything just to get off light. Let them. The consequence still exists, and a child who keeps choosing honesty because it works is learning exactly what you want him to learn. And what about the child who keeps lying anyway? Expect that for a while. Trust is built slowly, one kept promise at a time.

The very first hiding in Scripture happens in the garden. After Adam and Eve ate from the tree, they hid among the trees when they heard God walking there. God called out, Where are you? And Adam answered, I heard the sound of you in the garden, and I was afraid, and I hid myself. Fear and hiding have been tied together since the beginning. And notice that it was God who came looking. He did not wait for Adam to come out on his own. A father who goes looking, gently, makes it easier for a hiding child to step out.

Psalm one hundred three says the Lord does not deal with us according to our sins. As far as the east is from the west, so far does He remove our transgressions from us. That is why we can come to Him honestly. His mercy makes the truth safe to tell.

A father who makes the truth safe at home is preparing his children for something larger. One day they will kneel in a confessional. You want them to walk in expecting mercy, because that is what they found when they came to you.

So gather the kids today and make them that promise, in words they will remember. Then keep it, every single time.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is making the truth promise to your children. The promise is simple. In this house, telling the truth always makes it better. A child who confesses always gets a lighter consequence than a child who is caught. It works because it changes the math in a child's head, so that hiding no longer looks like the better bet.

Here is how to do it. Gather the kids at a calm time, maybe at dinner. Keep it short and warm. Say something like this. I want to make you a promise. In our family, telling the truth always makes things better. If you do something wrong and you come tell me, the consequence will always be smaller than if I find out another way. And I promise I won't yell at you for telling me the truth. Ask them to say the promise back to you.

Then give an example so they understand. If you break a glass and come tell me, we clean it up together and that's it. If you hide the pieces and I find them, there will be a bigger consequence for hiding.

Now the hard part, which is keeping it. When a child confesses, your first words are thanks. For example. Thank you for telling me. That took courage. Then take a breath, and handle the problem calmly, with the lighter consequence you promised.

Also, start from trust. When your child tells you something, believe them unless you have a real reason not to. Keep this promise every single time, especially when you are angry.
days.fact: In First Samuel chapter fourteen, King Saul swears that whoever eats before evening will die. His son Jonathan, not knowing of the oath, tastes a little honey. When Saul demands the truth, Jonathan admits it plainly, and Saul declares that he must die. In verse forty-five, the people refuse and rescue Jonathan. A son's honesty was met with a father's harshness, and others had to step in.

dailyVerse.text: Whoever hides his sins will not prosper, but whoever confesses and forsakes them will find mercy.

days.church: The Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraph twenty-four sixty-eight, teaches that truthfulness is the virtue of showing oneself true in deeds and truthful in words. Children grow in that virtue where honesty is safe. When telling the truth always makes things better in your home, you make truthfulness easier to choose, and you prepare your children to approach God's mercy without fear.

days.focus: Advent began Nov 29. Keep the system boring and predictable. Add an Advent family prayer at dinner.
days.verse: As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has compassion on those who fear Him.
days.title: St. Joseph's silence
days.teach: No word of St. Joseph is recorded in the Gospels. He protected, provided, and obeyed, and spoke through what he did. Advent invites that same silence. Protect your morning prayer this week, above all.
days.do: Fifteen minutes of morning silence before the house wakes.
days.ask: Where does my noise crowd out my example?
days.talk:
This week's psalm says that the Lord knows how we are made, and remembers that we are dust. He does not wait for us to be impressive. Today, on this Second Sunday of Advent, the Church sets before us a man who was never trying to be impressive at all.

No word of Saint Joseph is recorded in the Gospels. Not one. He is the head of the Holy Family, the man God trusted to raise His Son, and Scripture gives us nothing he said.

What it gives us instead is what he did. He protected. He provided. He obeyed. When the angel told him to take Mary into his home, he did. When he was warned to flee into Egypt, he rose in the night and took the child and his mother and went. When it was safe to return, he returned. Joseph spoke through what he did.

There is a lesson in that for a father trying to stop yelling. Much of what fills a noisy house is words. Instructions repeated four times. Lectures. Warnings. Commentary. We talk, and then talk louder, as if volume were the same as leadership. Joseph shows another way. A man steady enough that he did not need to fill the room.

Why do fathers fill the house with words? Because words feel like action. When a child is not listening, saying it again feels like doing something. And talking feels like control. A man who is uneasy inside often gets louder outside, as if more words could settle what is unsettled in him. Silence asks for a kind of steadiness that most of us have to practice.

Advent invites that same silence. It is a season of waiting, and waiting is quiet. The world around you is getting louder by the day, with shopping and parties and noise. The Church asks you to go the other direction.

So protect your morning prayer this week, above all. Get up before the house wakes. Before the phone, before the email, before the first child comes down the stairs. Sit in the quiet with God. Read the day's Gospel if you like, or say nothing at all. Let Him speak first.

Picture two mornings. In the first, the alarm goes off, and the first thing you see is your phone. Work email, the news, a message that annoys you. By the time the kids come down, your mind is already in three other places, and the first words out of your mouth are about being late. In the second, you get up a little early, make the coffee, and sit in your chair in the dark. You read a few lines of the Gospel. You say almost nothing. When the first child comes down the stairs, you are already there, and already quiet. The day starts from a different place.

The prophet Elijah learned where God speaks. He stood on the mountain, and a great wind tore at the rocks, but the Lord was not in the wind. Then came an earthquake, but the Lord was not in the earthquake. Then fire, but the Lord was not in the fire. And after the fire came a still small voice. That is where Elijah met Him. God can speak in thunder. But very often He chooses the quiet, and He waits for us to be quiet enough to hear.

Some fathers say they can't spare fifteen minutes. Try it for one week before deciding. Most men find the morning goes better, not worse, when it starts in quiet. Others say their mind wanders the whole time. That is normal. Every time you notice it wandering and gently come back, you have prayed. Nobody does this perfectly, and God is not grading you.

Think about where your noise crowds out your example. Where the words are many and the witness is thin. Jesus grew up in the house of a man whose life did the talking.

Your children will not remember most of what you said to them this Advent. They will remember what kind of man their father was. Was he steady? Did he keep his word? Did they find him praying when they came down the stairs?

Tomorrow morning, before anyone else is awake, give the first quarter hour of the day to silence and prayer.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is setting up tomorrow morning's fifteen minutes of silence, before the house wakes. It is a short, protected time to sit with God before the noise of the day begins. A father who starts the day quiet carries more steadiness into the morning rush.

Here is how to prepare tonight. Set your alarm fifteen minutes earlier than usual. Choose your spot, a chair in a quiet room, away from the kitchen traffic. Put your phone to charge in another room, and use a simple alarm clock if you need one. If you like, set out a Bible or a missal with the day's readings.

Tomorrow morning, get up, make your coffee, and go straight to your chair. Do not check messages or the news first. That is the rule that protects everything else.

Then follow a simple pattern. Make the sign of the cross. Read the day's Gospel slowly, or a short psalm. Then sit in silence for several minutes. Let God speak first. You do not need to fill the time with words. If your mind wanders, gently come back.

End with a short offering, in your own words. For example. Lord, here is my day. Help me speak less and show more. Or. Saint Joseph, pray for me, that my life does the talking.

If a child wakes early and finds you, let them sit with you quietly. That is not an interruption. That is the lesson. Do this every morning this week.
days.fact: In Isaiah chapter 63, verse 16, the prophet prays, You, Lord, are our Father. The Old Testament rarely addresses God this directly as Father in prayer, which makes the line stand out. The Church reads it last Sunday, the First Sunday of Advent this year. Advent begins with a people admitting they need a Father, which is a good place for any father to begin too.

dailyVerse.text: When Joseph rose from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him and took Mary his wife into his home.

days.church: The Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs five thirty-one and five thirty-two, teaches that for most of His life Jesus shared the hidden life of Nazareth, and that He was obedient to Mary and Joseph. Those quiet years under Joseph's roof were not wasted. A father who keeps silence and prayer before the house wakes is learning from the hidden life of the Holy Family.

days.focus: Immaculate Conception, Dec 8. Review points with your wife; adjust targets that are too easy or too hard.
days.verse: Teach them diligently to your children, when you sit in your house and when you walk by the way.
days.title: Real responsibility
days.teach: Chores build competence and a sense of belonging. Give real jobs that matter to the family, not busywork, and praise them specifically. A kid who is needed behaves differently.
days.do: Give each kid one meaningful chore.
days.ask: Do my kids feel needed here?
days.talk:
This week's Scripture comes from Deuteronomy. Teach them diligently to your children, when you sit in your house and when you walk by the way. Today, that teaching happens with a trash bag and a dog bowl.

Chores have a bad reputation in most houses. They are something kids get nagged into, and parents end up doing them because it is faster. But chores done well build two things your children need. Competence, the sense that they can actually do hard things. And belonging, the sense that this family needs them.

Why do so many fathers give up on chores? Because doing it yourself is faster, and quieter. Because the nagging wears everyone out, and it seems easier to skip the fight. And because many of us remember chores as punishment, something handed out when we were in trouble. So we either do the work ourselves, or we hand out jobs that don't matter just to keep the kids busy. Neither builds anything.

The key word is real. Busywork doesn't do it. Kids can tell when a job is fake. Sorting the junk drawer so they stay out of your hair teaches them that they are being managed. A real job is one the family actually depends on. Feeding the dog, when the dog really does go hungry if it doesn't happen. Taking out the trash on trash night. Setting the table for dinner. Caring for the animals. Packing their own gear for practice. If the job didn't get done, someone would notice.

Picture dinnertime going wrong. You are setting the table yourself, muttering, while the kids are on screens in the next room. Finally you bark at them to come help. They shuffle in, slow and resentful, and you end up redoing half of it anyway. Now picture it going right. The kitchen timer goes off, and your daughter knows the table is her job. She sets it without being asked. She forgets the forks, but she remembered the napkins, and you tell her so. She goes back for the forks on her own, and she sits down at dinner a little taller than usual.

When they do it, praise them specifically. Skip the generic good job. Say something like, the table looked great tonight, and you remembered the napkins. Specific praise tells them exactly what they did right, and that you saw it. Praise like that does something a reward never can. It tells a child that his work was noticed by the person whose opinion matters most to him. Start small. One real job per child is plenty.

What if they do it badly? At first, they will. Resist the urge to redo it in front of them. Teach the next step the next day, and let the job get better over time. A crooked place setting that a child did himself is worth more than a perfect one you did for him. And what if a child refuses? Treat it like any other instruction. Say it once, calmly, and follow through with a small consequence. But most refusals fade once the job is tied to a fixed time and stops being a surprise.

Here is the deeper point. A kid who is needed behaves differently. A child who knows the household relies on him has a reason to cooperate that has nothing to do with fear of punishment. He is part of something. That is a strong motive, and most of us barely use it.

Go back to Deuteronomy. When you sit in your house and when you walk by the way. Much of that teaching happens in ordinary work done side by side. Showing a child how to do a job properly, then trusting him to do it, is exactly that kind of teaching.

Remember that the Son of God spent most of His years on earth doing ordinary work. The people of Nazareth called Him the carpenter, and the carpenter's son. Jesus learned a trade in Joseph's workshop, by watching and then by doing, the way every apprentice learns. The Church honors Joseph as the patron of workers. Ordinary work, done well inside a family, is holy ground.

Ask yourself whether your kids feel needed here. Then today, hand each of them one job that genuinely matters to the family.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is giving each child one real chore. A real chore is a job the family actually depends on, so if it doesn't get done, someone would notice. It works because a child who is needed has a reason to cooperate that has nothing to do with fear, and doing it well builds the sense that they can handle hard things.

Here is how to do it. First, choose one job per child that fits their age and truly matters. Some examples. Feeding the dog every morning. Taking the trash and recycling to the curb on pickup night. Setting the table for dinner. Unloading the dishwasher. Packing their own bag for school or practice. Helping make one simple part of dinner.

Second, teach it side by side. Do it with them the first time and show each step. Then watch them do it while you help. Then let them do it alone. Explain why it matters. For example. The dog counts on you. He has nobody else to feed him in the morning.

Third, tie it to a fixed time, so it doesn't need nagging. The table gets set when the timer goes off for dinner. The trash goes out right after Thursday dinner.

Fourth, use labeled praise, which means praise that names exactly what they did. For example. The table looked great tonight, and you remembered the napkins. Thanks for getting the bins out without a reminder. The whole house runs better because of that.

Hand each child their job today, and start tonight.
days.fact: In First Samuel chapter sixteen, verse eleven, when Samuel comes to anoint a son of Jesse, the youngest, David, is not even present. He is out keeping the sheep. In chapter seventeen, David tells Saul that while guarding his father's flock he chased down a lion and a bear to rescue a lamb. A real job entrusted by his father had trained the future king.

dailyVerse.text: Whatever you do, do it from the heart, as working for the Lord and not for men.

days.church: The Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraph twenty-four twenty-seven, teaches that human work honors the Creator, and it recalls that Jesus Himself worked as a carpenter at Nazareth. When you hand your child a real job and teach it side by side, you pass on more than a chore. You show him that ordinary work, done well for his family, can be offered to God.

days.focus: Immaculate Conception, Dec 8. Review points with your wife; adjust targets that are too easy or too hard.
days.verse: Teach them diligently to your children, when you sit in your house and when you walk by the way.
days.title: Immaculate Conception: honor your wife
days.teach: Children's sense of security is tied to how their parents treat each other. Honor your wife in front of them. Mary's yes changed a household. Your daily yes to your marriage steadies yours.
days.do: Praise your wife to the kids, in her hearing.
days.ask: Do my kids see me cherish their mother?
days.talk:
Today is the Solemnity of the Immaculate Conception. The Church celebrates that Mary, from the first moment of her conception, was preserved from original sin, made ready by God for the yes she would one day give.

That yes changed a household. When Mary consented to God's plan, it reshaped her life, and Joseph's life, and the home they would make in Nazareth. Everything about that small family was built on her yes, and on his.

Your household is built on a yes too. The one you said at the altar, and the one you keep saying every day. Here is something every father should take seriously. Children's sense of security is tied to how their parents treat each other. Kids watch their parents' marriage the way sailors watch the sky. When it is calm between you and your wife, they feel it. When there is tension, they feel that too, even when you think you are hiding it.

Why do so many good husbands stop saying kind things out loud? Not because the love is gone. Usually because the years turn a marriage into logistics. Who is picking up whom. What is for dinner. Whether the bill got paid. The admiration is still there, but it goes quiet, because the day is full and nobody stops to say it. And some of us grew up in homes where kind words between parents were simply never spoken in front of the children.

So honor your wife in front of them. Not only in private. Out loud, where they can hear. Tell them what she does for this family that they may not notice. The things she carries. The way she loves them. Let them hear their father speak of their mother with real respect and real affection.

Picture dinner going one way. Your wife sets the food on the table, and you look up from your phone to mention that the milk is gone again. Nobody means anything by it. But the kids absorb it. Now picture it going another way. Before anyone eats, you say, Hey, did everyone notice that Mom got all three of you to practice today and still made this? Let's thank her. She waves it off. But she smiles. And your children look at their mother, for a moment, through your eyes.

This does two things. It steadies your children, because a child who sees his parents cherish each other knows the ground under him is solid. And it shows them what a marriage looks like from the inside. If you have a son, he is learning how a man treats his wife. If you have a daughter, she is learning what she should expect.

What if it feels forced? Then say only what is true, and say it simply. You are not giving a speech. One honest sentence is enough. And what if things are tense between you right now? Then look for something small that is still true, and say that. Honest respect in a hard season can do more than grand words in an easy one. It may even be the first step toward warmer days between the two of you.

Saint Paul gave husbands a hard standard. Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the Church and gave himself up for her. He did not say, love your wives when it is convenient, or when they deserve it. He pointed to the Cross. Praising your wife in front of your children is a small thing compared to that. But it is the same kind of love, the kind that puts her honor ahead of your own comfort.

Your wife may be surprised the first time. She may laugh it off, or wonder what you are after. That is fine. Say it again next week, and the week after. What begins as a surprise becomes part of the air your children breathe. And notice what it does to you. A man who looks for what is good in his wife, so that he can say it out loud, starts to see more of it.

Ask yourself honestly whether your kids see you cherish their mother, or mostly see the two of you managing logistics.

Your daily yes to your marriage steadies your whole home. So today, with your wife close enough to hear, tell the kids something good and true about her.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is praising your wife to your children, out loud, while she can hear you. It works because children feel secure when they see their parents cherish each other, and because they learn what a marriage should look like by watching yours.

Here is how to do it. First, think of something specific and true. Something she does for this family that the kids may not notice, or a quality you admire in her. Second, pick a moment when the kids are present and she is within earshot. Dinner works well. So does the car. Third, say it plainly and warmly, then let it stand. No joke at her expense, no sarcasm, and no but.

Some examples. Did you guys notice that Mom remembered every single one of your practices this week? She keeps this whole family running. Or. I want you to know your mom is the kindest person I know. I learn from her every day. Or. Your mother worked hard on this dinner. Let's thank her. Or. One of the best decisions I ever made was marrying your mom.

If she looks surprised, or if the kids roll their eyes, keep going. It may feel unusual at first. Make it normal.

Later tonight, you can tell her directly too, just the two of you. And if your marriage is in a hard season right now, look for something small that is still true, and say that. Children notice honest respect, even more than grand words.
days.fact: In Ruth chapter three, verse eleven, Boaz tells Ruth that everyone in his town knows she is a woman of worth. The Hebrew phrase is eshet chayil, a woman of strength or valor, the same phrase that opens the poem of the capable wife in Proverbs chapter thirty-one, verse ten. Boaz honored her character publicly, and their son Obed became the grandfather of King David.

dailyVerse.text: Mary said, Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.

days.church: The Church teaches, as a dogma defined by Pope Pius the Ninth in eighteen fifty-four, that Mary was preserved from all stain of original sin from the first moment of her conception. The Catechism of the Catholic Church treats this in paragraphs four ninety to four ninety-three. God prepared her to give her free yes. Today, honor the mother of your own children where they can hear.

days.focus: Immaculate Conception, Dec 8. Review points with your wife; adjust targets that are too easy or too hard.
days.verse: Teach them diligently to your children, when you sit in your house and when you walk by the way.
days.title: Adjust the chart
days.teach: Review the targets with your wife. Move mastered behaviors off the chart, keep praising them, and add one new target. A chart that never changes goes stale.
days.do: Make one swap on each kid's chart.
days.ask: Which behavior has actually changed?
days.talk:
Teach them diligently to your children. That is this week's word from Deuteronomy, and today the word that matters most is diligently.

A behavior chart is a tool, and like any tool, it needs maintenance. A chart that never changes goes stale. The kids stop seeing it. The points stop meaning anything. What started as a game becomes wallpaper.

Why do charts go stale? Mostly because they work. Once things improve, a father stops looking closely. The crisis that made him pay attention is gone, the chart sits on the refrigerator, and nobody quite notices that the targets on it no longer fit the child in front of him. Success, oddly enough, is often what lets a good tool slip.

So today, sit down with your wife and review the targets. Look at each behavior on each child's chart and ask a simple question. Has this actually changed? Not whether it went well yesterday. Whether it has changed, reliably, over weeks.

Picture a chart that has been on the refrigerator for six weeks without a single change. Your son checks off getting dressed before breakfast every morning without even thinking. The point means nothing to him anymore, and the one behavior that still causes fights every evening is not on the chart at all. Now picture a Sunday night conversation instead. You tell him getting dressed is mastered, and that you are proud of him. You take it off together. Then you add the evening fight as a new target, and he is a little excited, because he knows he can win at this.

Where the answer is yes, move that behavior off the chart. That is a win worth celebrating. But don't stop praising it. A behavior that disappears from the chart and from your attention at the same time can quietly slide back. Keep noticing it out loud, even without points attached. Make the retirement a small celebration. A high five, a favorite dessert, a phone call to a grandparent to share the news. Graduating a behavior should feel like a promotion, not like losing the points.

Then add one new target in its place. Just one. Choose something that matters, that the child can actually do, and that you can see clearly enough to count. Some targets will have turned out too easy, and some too hard. Adjust them. A target a child hits every day without effort teaches nothing. A target he never hits teaches him to quit trying.

Bring the children into the change. Ask each one, What do you think you're ready to work on next? You and your wife keep the final say, but let their idea count. A child who helps pick the goal is far more likely to own it.

What if you retire a behavior and it slides back? Then put it back on for a couple of weeks. That is not failure. That is the chart doing its job. And what if you and your wife disagree about whether something is truly mastered? Go with the more cautious view, and look again next week. The two of you are a team on this, and the children should see one chart, not two opinions. Better one more week of points than a rule that quietly falls apart.

Think of the way a good doctor manages a medication. When a patient responds, he doesn't leave him on the same dose forever without looking. He reassesses, tapers what is no longer needed, and addresses what is still unresolved. The chart deserves the same attention.

Deuteronomy tells fathers to keep God's words on their hearts and teach them diligently to their children. Diligence in teaching means paying attention to where the child actually is today, not where he was two months ago.

Saint Paul understood this kind of teaching. He wrote to the Christians at Corinth that he had fed them with milk, not solid food, because they were not yet ready for it. A good teacher gives what the student can take in now, and then moves him forward. Your children are growing every week. What they need from you should grow too.

Ask yourself which behavior has truly changed. Then today, with your wife, make one trade on each child's chart. Retire a win, and give them a fresh goal to reach for.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is adjusting the point chart with your wife. A point chart is a simple chart for each child listing a few target behaviors, where the child earns a point, a check, or a sticker each time they do one, and the points add up to small rewards. Like any tool, it needs maintenance, or it turns into wallpaper.

Sit down with your wife and each child's chart for fifteen minutes. Go behavior by behavior and ask one question. Has this really changed, reliably, over the past couple of weeks?

If yes, retire it. Take it off the chart and celebrate the win with the child. For example. You've been getting dressed before breakfast every day without a reminder. That's mastered. We're taking it off the chart. Then keep noticing it out loud, with no points attached, so it doesn't quietly slide back.

If a behavior is too easy, make it a little harder. If a child never earns it, make it smaller. For example. Instead of homework done without complaining, try starting homework by four thirty.

Then add one new target in place of the one you retired. Make it positive, specific, and easy to see. Some examples. Shoes and backpack by the door before bed. Speaking kindly to a sibling when frustrated. Putting dishes in the sink after every meal. Getting into bed when the timer rings.

Make one trade on each child's chart, and tell each child about the change today, with something warm about what they have already done.
days.fact: First Samuel chapter two, verse twenty-six, says the boy Samuel kept growing, both in stature and in favor with the Lord and with people. Luke later describes the boy Jesus in almost the same words. Scripture marks a child's growth in stages, noticing over time how he is changing. Even in the shadow of Eli's failing household, Samuel's growth was seen and recorded.

dailyVerse.text: I gave you milk to drink, not solid food, because you were not yet ready for it.

days.church: The Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraph twenty-two twenty-one, teaches that the role of parents in education is so important that it can hardly be replaced, and that their right and duty to educate is primordial and inalienable. Reviewing the chart with your wife is part of that duty. Teaching well means meeting each child where he is today and helping him take the next step.

days.verse: Teach them diligently to your children, when you sit in your house and when you walk by the way.
days.title: Fathers and sons
days.teach: Many boys talk most easily side by side rather than face to face: building, driving, working on a project together. A son needs a father who believes him and believes in him. Your belief becomes part of how he sees himself.
days.do: Do one side-by-side activity with your son.
days.ask: Does he know I believe in him?
days.talk:
This week's Scripture tells fathers to teach their children when you sit in your house and when you walk by the way. Today, the emphasis falls on the walking.

Many boys talk most easily side by side rather than face to face. Sit a boy across a table, look him in the eye, and ask how he is doing, and you may get one word. Put him next to you with a wrench in his hand, working on a bike, and twenty minutes later he may be telling you about the thing that has bothered him all week.

Face to face can feel like an interview, or worse, like being in trouble. Side by side, the pressure comes off. The task gives you both somewhere to look. Silence is comfortable instead of awkward. Words come when they are ready.

Why do fathers default to face to face? Because that is how most of us learned a serious conversation is supposed to look. Across a desk. Across a kitchen table. Eye contact, direct questions, a clear answer. It works in a meeting at work. With a son, it often works against you. The harder you press for words, the faster the door closes.

So find ways to be next to your son. Building something. Driving somewhere with no hurry. Working on a project in the garage. Fixing something that is broken. Don't fill the time with questions. Let the work carry it, and listen when he talks.

Picture it going wrong. A report card comes home, and you sit him down at the table. How's school going? Fine. Anything bothering you? No. A long silence. He looks at the door, and the conversation is over almost before it began. Now picture a Saturday afternoon instead. You are raking leaves, and he is holding the bag. Nobody is asking him anything. Somewhere around the third pile he mentions a kid on the bus who has been giving him a hard time. You keep raking. You say, Sounds like that's been getting to you. And he keeps going.

Deuteronomy tells fathers to teach their children when you sit in your house and when you walk by the way. Notice how much of that is shoulder to shoulder. Walking along a road together. Doing ordinary things together. Passing faith from father to son was never meant to be mainly a lecture across a table.

What if he still doesn't talk? That is fine. The time together is the point, not the conversation. A boy who spends regular hours next to his father learns that his father is there, and the words will come in their own season. And what if you are not handy? It doesn't matter. Washing the car, shooting baskets, a slow drive to the hardware store. The skill is not in the task. It is in being next to him.

Think of the two disciples on the road to Emmaus after the Crucifixion. They were discouraged and confused, and the risen Lord came and walked beside them. He did not sit them down. He walked with them along the road and opened the Scriptures to them as they went. Afterward they said to each other, Did not our hearts burn within us while He talked to us on the road?

Underneath all of this is something bigger. Your son needs a father who believes him and believes in him. Believes him, meaning when he tells you something, you take him at his word. Believes in him, meaning you see what he can become and you let him know it. Both matter, and he needs both from you.

Some of the best conversations a father ever has with his son happen in a car at night, headlights on the road, neither of you looking at the other. Don't fill those drives with the radio or the phone. Leave the quiet open, and see what he puts into it. And days later, mention what he told you, so he knows it stayed with you.

Your belief becomes part of how he sees himself. The voice he hears in his own head, years from now, will sound a lot like yours.

So ask yourself whether he knows you believe in him. Then today, find something to do with your son, shoulder to shoulder.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is a side by side activity with your son. Side by side means working on something next to him, shoulder to shoulder, rather than sitting across from him and asking questions. Many boys talk most easily when their hands are busy and their eyes have somewhere to look, so the pressure comes off.

Here is how to do it. First, choose something real that takes at least twenty minutes. Some examples. Washing the car. Fixing a bike or a broken toy. Building something in the garage. Cooking dinner together. Raking leaves or shoveling snow. Shooting baskets. A drive to the hardware store with no hurry.

Second, invite him plainly. For example. I'm going to work on the bike chain. Want to give me a hand? Third, let the work carry the time. Do not interview him. Silence is fine. If he talks, listen, and reflect back what you hear. For example. Sounds like that kid at school has been getting on your nerves. Then let him keep going, or let it drop.

Fourth, before you finish, say one sentence that shows you believe in him. For example. You're really good at figuring out how things work. Or. I like doing this with you. You're a hard worker. And if he tells you something, believe him. Take him at his word.

If you have no son, do this with a daughter. It works for many children. If you have more than one son, give each his own time this week. Start with one today.
days.fact: In Mark chapter nine, a father brings his suffering son to Jesus. Before acting, Jesus asks the father how long this has been happening, and the father answers, since childhood. When Jesus speaks of faith, the father cries out, in verse twenty-four, that he believes and begs help for his unbelief. Jesus honored a father's honest, imperfect belief and healed his son.

dailyVerse.text: While they were talking and reasoning together, Jesus Himself drew near and walked along with them.

days.church: The Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs twenty-two thirty-two and twenty-two thirty-three, teaches that family ties are important but not absolute, and that each child has his own vocation. Your son is not a copy of you. Believing in him means watching for who God is calling him to become, and telling him what you see. Your confidence helps him hear that call.

days.focus: Immaculate Conception, Dec 8. Review points with your wife; adjust targets that are too easy or too hard.
days.verse: Teach them diligently to your children, when you sit in your house and when you walk by the way.
days.title: Fathers and daughters
days.teach: A daughter learns from her father what a good man's attention feels like. Listen without fixing. Show up to what she loves. Ask about her world and remember the details.
days.do: Ask your daughter about her week and follow up on one detail tomorrow.
days.ask: What's the last thing she told me that I remembered?
days.talk:
This week Deuteronomy has told you to teach your children when you sit in your house and when you walk by the way. Some of the most important teaching a father does is not in words at all. It is in the kind of attention he gives.

A daughter learns from her father what a good man's attention feels like. That is a weighty sentence, and it is true. The way you listen to her now becomes a standard she carries into her friendships and, one day, into deciding whom to trust.

So what does good attention look like? It starts with listening without fixing. When your daughter tells you about a hard practice or a friend who was unkind, your instinct is to diagnose and fix. Hold off. Most of the time she isn't asking for a plan. She wants to know that you heard her and that it mattered to you. Ask a question instead of giving an answer.

Why is that instinct so strong? Because many men show love by solving problems. When someone we love is hurting, fixing it feels like the most caring thing we can do. But to a daughter, a quick fix can sound like, this isn't worth more of my time. The solution may be right. The timing tells her something else.

Picture it going wrong. She comes home upset because her friends left her out at lunch. You tell her to just find some new friends, those girls aren't worth it anyway. She says never mind, and goes upstairs. Now picture it going right. You say, That sounds really hard. What happened? She tells you more. Then more. You never offer a single solution. The next morning, in the car, you ask whether lunch was any better. She looks at you, a little surprised that you remembered.

Next, show up to what she loves. Be at the game, the recital, the barn or the field. Watch her play, perform, or ride. Learn enough about what she does that you can ask a real question about it. Your presence at the rail says something words cannot.

Then ask about her world and remember the details. The name of the girl at school. The part of practice that gave her trouble. The thing she was nervous about on Tuesday. Bring it back up later. Few things tell a child she matters more than discovering that her father remembered. And put the phone away when she is talking. Nothing tells a girl more plainly where she ranks than whether her father's eyes stay on her or drift to a screen.

A daughter who has known her father's patient, interested attention is harder to fool later on. She knows what it feels like to be taken seriously by a good man, and she will notice when it is missing.

What if she won't talk to you? Some seasons are like that, especially as she gets older. Keep showing up anyway. Keep asking small questions, and keep listening when the answers are short. The door often opens later than you would like, but it opens for the father who kept knocking. And what if she really does want advice? Ask her. Do you want my help with this, or do you just want me to listen? She will tell you, and either way she will know you asked.

Think of Jairus in the Gospel of Mark. He was a leader of the synagogue, a man of standing in his town. He fell at the feet of Jesus and begged Him to come, because his little daughter was dying. Then Jesus took the girl by the hand and raised her up. A father who would kneel in the road for his daughter is the kind of father she deserves.

And notice what Jesus said right after the miracle. He told them to give her something to eat. In the middle of the most astonishing thing anyone in that house had ever seen, He paid attention to a small, ordinary need of a twelve year old girl. Great love often shows itself in small details.

Ask yourself honestly what the last thing she told you was, and whether you remembered it.

Today, ask your daughter about her week and really listen. Then hold on to one thing she says, and bring it up with her tomorrow.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is asking your daughter about her week, really listening, and then bringing back one detail tomorrow. Few things tell a child she matters more than discovering that her father remembered what she said.

Here is how to do it. First, find a calm moment with just the two of you. The car, a walk, bedtime, or a quiet minute in the kitchen. Put your phone away.

Second, ask specific questions, not just how was your week. Some examples. What was the best part of your week? Who did you sit with at lunch? What was hard at practice? Is anything coming up that you're nervous about?

Third, listen without fixing. If she tells you about a problem, resist the urge to solve it. Ask one more question instead. For example. That sounds really hard. What happened next? Or. How did that make you feel? Reflect back what you hear, and let her lead.

Fourth, after the conversation, pick one detail and write it down where you will see it tomorrow. A name, an upcoming test, a part of practice that worried her, something a friend said.

Tomorrow, bring it up. For example. Hey, how did the spelling test go? Or. Did your friend ever say sorry? Or. Was practice any better today? Then listen again.

If you have no daughter, do this with any of your children. If you have more than one daughter, give each her own conversation this week, starting with one today.
days.fact: In Mark chapter five, verse twenty-three, Jairus begs Jesus to come because his little daughter is dying. Mark's Greek uses thugatrion, an affectionate diminutive, something like my little girl. When Jesus raises her in verse forty-one, Mark keeps His Aramaic words, talitha koum, which he translates as little girl, arise. The tenderness of a father's pet name is preserved in the text.

dailyVerse.text: Taking the child by the hand, He said to her, Talitha cumi, which means, Little girl, I say to you, arise.

days.church: The Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraph twenty-two twenty-eight, teaches that parents show respect and affection for their children through the care and attention they give in raising them. Attention is a form of love your daughter can feel. Listening without fixing, showing up to what she loves, and remembering what she told you are ways of giving that care every ordinary day.

days.focus: Immaculate Conception, Dec 8. Review points with your wife; adjust targets that are too easy or too hard.
days.verse: Teach them diligently to your children, when you sit in your house and when you walk by the way.
days.title: Guilt vs. shame
days.teach: Shame ("I'm a bad father") makes people defensive and reactive. Guilt ("I did something wrong") leads to repair. Confession turns one into the other. Bring the yelling there, and leave with the grace to try again.
days.do: Go to Confession this week if you haven't this month.
days.ask: Am I carrying shame that keeps me reactive?
days.talk:
This week Deuteronomy has told fathers that God's words should be upon their hearts. Today we look at what else a father carries on his heart, and what he can do with it.

There are two very different voices that can follow a bad moment. One says, I am a bad father. The other says, I did something wrong. They sound similar. They lead to completely different places.

The first voice is shame. Shame is about who you are, and it makes people defensive and reactive. If you believe you are a bad father, every one of your child's misbehaviors becomes a verdict on you. Every bit of back talk feels like proof. You get prickly, you overreact, you yell, and then the shame gets heavier. It is a loop, and it feeds the very thing you are trying to stop.

Why do good fathers carry so much of it? Partly because they care. A man who did not love his children would not lose sleep over raising his voice. And partly because men tend to carry these things alone. We replay the bad moment in private, compare ourselves to the father we wanted to be, and never say a word about it to anyone. Shame grows best in the dark.

The second voice is guilt. Guilt is about what you did. It is specific, and it points somewhere. I yelled at him in front of his friend. That was wrong. I can apologize, I can make it right, and I can do better tomorrow. Guilt leads to repair.

Picture two fathers after the same hard bedtime. Both yelled. The first sits downstairs replaying it, thinking he is just like his own father and will never change. The next morning he is short with everyone, and when his wife mentions the night before, he snaps at her too. The second father names it to himself. I lost my temper at bedtime. In the morning he says to his son, I yelled last night. That was wrong, and I'm sorry. On Saturday he goes to Confession. Same failure. Very different next day.

Confession is where one turns into the other. You walk in carrying the vague, heavy weight of being the kind of father who yells. You name the specific things you did. You hear the words of absolution, and your sins are forgiven. And you walk out with something shame never gives you, the grace to try again.

What if you have confessed the same thing many times already? So has nearly every Catholic who has ever lived. That is not a reason to stay away. It is the reason the sacrament is there to be received again and again. And what if it has been years? Simply tell the priest it has been a long time. He will help you. Priests are glad to see a man come back. Many of them will tell you it is the best part of their week.

King David knew both voices. After his great sin, when the prophet Nathan confronted him, David did not hide behind excuses. He said plainly, I have sinned against the Lord. The psalm the Church has long associated with that moment is a cry of guilt that leads somewhere. Create in me a clean heart, O God, and put a new and right spirit within me.

Remember Peter after he denied knowing the Lord three times. After the Resurrection, on the shore of the sea, Jesus asked him three times whether he loved Him. Three denials, and three chances to answer. Jesus did not leave Peter buried in what he had done. He gave him back his mission. Feed my sheep.

Bring the repair home, too. If you have not already, go to the child you yelled at. Keep it short. Name what you did, say you are sorry, and tell him what you will try to do instead. You are not handing him your burden. You are showing him what a man does after he gets it wrong. That may be the most important lesson he learns from you this month.

Ask yourself if you are carrying shame that keeps you reactive. If you are, don't carry it another week. Bring the yelling to the confessional.

If it has been more than a month, find a time for Confession in the next few days, and go.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is planning to go to Confession this week, if you have not been in the past month. Confession, the sacrament of Penance, is where vague shame about being the kind of father who yells becomes specific guilt that can be forgiven, so you walk out with the grace to try again.

Here is how to do it. First, find a time. Check your parish bulletin or website for confession hours, often Saturday afternoon or before a weekday Mass. Many parishes also hear confessions by appointment. Put the time on your calendar today.

Second, prepare by naming specifics. Shame is general. Guilt is specific. Instead of I've been a bad father, name the actual acts. For example. I yelled at my children in anger many times this month. I spoke harshly to my wife in front of the kids. I was impatient and sarcastic with my son when he struggled. I neglected prayer with my family. Write a short list if that helps.

Third, go. Tell the priest how long it has been since your last confession, confess your sins plainly, listen to his counsel, receive your penance, and pray an Act of Contrition. If you have forgotten the words, most confessionals have a card, or you can simply say you are sorry in your own words.

Fourth, do your penance soon, ideally right after.

If you went recently, pray an Act of Contrition tonight instead, and ask for the grace to be slow to anger.
days.fact: The heading of Psalm fifty-one ties it to the time the prophet Nathan confronted David over Bathsheba. In Second Samuel chapter twelve, verse thirteen, David admits he has sinned against the Lord, and Nathan tells him the Lord has put away his sin. The psalm asks God to create a clean heart in him. Specific confession, not despair, opened the way to restoration.

dailyVerse.text: If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just, and will forgive our sins and cleanse us from all wrongdoing.

days.church: The Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraph fourteen fifty-eight, teaches that regular confession of everyday faults, our venial sins, is strongly recommended, because it helps form conscience and fight evil tendencies. Canon nine eighty-nine requires confession of grave sins at least once a year. You need not wait for something grave. Bring your yelling to Confession, and receive forgiveness and the grace to begin again.
