days.title: Christmas Eve
days.teach: "For God so loved the world that He gave His only Son." The Father's gift was presence. Your kids will forget most of their presents. They won't forget whether you were there and calm. The biggest threat tonight is not a meltdown. It's the phone.
days.do: Put the phone away for the evening.
days.ask: What will they remember about tonight?
days.talk:
It is Christmas Eve. The house is full of wrapping paper, cooking, and anticipation. Before the evening takes over, take a moment with these words. For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son.

Think about what the Father gave. Not a thing. A presence. He did not send a message or a gift from a distance. He gave his Son, and the Son came. He entered a human family, a small house, a real life, and stayed. The gift of Christmas is God being with us.

Matthew gives the child a name that says exactly this. Emmanuel, which means God with us. And notice the sign the angel gave the shepherds that night. Not a palace, not a throne, but a baby wrapped in swaddling clothes and lying in a manger. God's greatest gift came in the plainest possible form. Someone you could find, and hold, and be near.

That tells you something about what your kids most need from you tonight. Your kids will forget most of their presents. Think about your own childhood. You may remember one or two gifts. But you probably remember whether your father was there, and what he was like. Whether he was calm or tense. Whether he laughed. Whether he seemed glad to be with you.

That is what your children will carry from tonight. Not the toys under the tree, but whether you were there and calm. Whether you sat on the floor and played. Whether you held the baby Jesus figure up for the youngest relative to place in the manger. Whether you walked into Mass with them, unhurried, and sang.

The biggest threat to that is not usually a meltdown. It is the phone. The work email that needs a quick answer. The texts about tomorrow's plans. Each one takes you out of the room for a moment, and those moments add up. Tonight, the most generous thing you can give your family is the thing God gave the world. Yourself, fully present.

Why is the phone so hard to set down, even tonight? Partly it is habit. Your hand reaches for it before you decide anything. Partly it is responsibility. Many fathers are the ones who coordinate the plans, answer the relatives, and keep an eye on work. Every buzz feels like a small duty calling. None of those duties is wrong. But together they can quietly take your whole evening, one glance at a time.

Picture two Christmas Eves. In the first, a father spends the evening half in the room. He checks a message during the reading from Luke, answers another while the kids show him their new pajamas, and steps into the hallway for a call about tomorrow. Nobody complains. But his son stops bringing things to show him by eight o'clock. In the second, the phone is in a drawer upstairs. The same father is on the floor, laughing too loud at the same old jokes, and his son falls asleep on his shoulder during the drive home from Mass.

You may worry about emergencies. Let someone who might need to reach you call your wife's phone instead. You may want pictures. Take one or two early in the evening, and then put the phone away. Your children do not need a perfect record of tonight nearly as much as they need you in it.

Here is a simple test for the evening. Every time you feel the pull to check something, look instead at one of your children and notice one thing about them. What they are laughing at. What they are holding. How they have grown since last Christmas. Let the urge to check become a reminder to look. Your attention is the gift tonight, and it is the one gift that cannot be bought in a store or wrapped in paper.

Think of Joseph at the manger. Scripture gives him no lines that night. He was simply there, guarding a mother and child in a stable, present to the most important night in history. That is the father's place tonight too. Not managing everything from the edge of the room, but kneeling in the middle of it.

So ask yourself one question before the evening begins. What will they remember about tonight? Then make it something good.

Put the phone away for the evening. Somewhere out of reach. Let tonight be a night when your children have all of you.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is putting the phone away for the evening. Not on silent in your pocket. Away. Somewhere out of reach, for the whole of Christmas Eve. It works because presence is the gift your children will actually remember, and the phone is what most often pulls a father out of the room.

Here is how to do it. Before the evening begins, take care of anything that truly cannot wait. Send the one message that needs sending. Then tell your wife your plan, and if someone may need to reach you in an emergency, let them call her phone. Put yours in a drawer, in the car, or on a high shelf in your bedroom. Leave it there until the kids are asleep.

Then fill the space it leaves. Sit on the floor and play with whatever comes out of the boxes. Let the youngest child place the baby Jesus in the manger. Walk into Mass together, unhurried, and sing. Read the Christmas story from Luke's Gospel aloud. Laugh at the same jokes again.

If you want a photo, take one or two early, then put the phone away. Your children do not need a record of the night as much as they need you in it.

If you feel the itch to check it, notice it, and let it pass. Ask yourself instead what your children will remember about tonight. Whether you were there, and whether you were calm. Give them all of you.
days.fact: In Isaiah chapter 9, verse 6, in some Bibles numbered verse 5, the prophet announces a child born for us and lists his names. One of them is Everlasting Father. This passage is read at the Christmas Mass during the Night. The Hebrew means, quite literally, father forever. The title does not make the Son the Father. It names the fatherly care the promised king shows his people for all time, and the Church hears it fulfilled in the child in the manger.

dailyVerse.text: God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.

days.church: The Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraph five twenty-five, teaches that Jesus was born in the humility of a stable, into a poor family, and that simple shepherds were the first witnesses. Paragraph five twenty-six adds that to enter the Kingdom we must become little, like children. The glory of Christmas came in plain presence. Tonight your children need the same from you, a father who is simply there.

days.title: Christmas: bless them
days.teach: Fathers have long blessed their children by tracing the sign of the cross on each child's forehead. It takes ten seconds. It tells a child he belongs to God and is loved by his father, and it closes even a hard day with peace. Start tonight and keep doing it.
days.do: Bless each child at bedtime.
days.ask: What do I want to speak over their lives?
days.talk:
Merry Christmas. Today is a day of feasting and family, and in the middle of it, there is something simple you can begin.

Fathers have long blessed their children by tracing the sign of the cross on each child's forehead. It is one of the oldest and simplest things a Christian father can do. You place your thumb on your child's forehead, trace the cross, and say a few words. God bless you. Or, May the Lord keep you. Or simply the child's name and the sign of the cross. It takes ten seconds.

Blessing children runs all through Scripture. In the Old Testament, Isaac blessed Jacob, and Jacob in his old age blessed each of his sons and grandsons. God gave Moses words for Aaron to speak over the people. The Lord bless you and keep you. The Lord make his face to shine upon you. And in the Gospels, when parents brought their children to Jesus, he took them in his arms, laid his hands on them, and blessed them.

Why does something so small matter? Because a blessing is a father speaking over his child's life. It tells a child, in a way words alone can't, that he belongs to God and is loved by his father. It is a moment of touch, attention, and faith all at once. Children who are blessed every night grow up with a sense that their father sees them, and hopes good things for them, and places them in God's hands.

So why do so many good Catholic fathers never do it? Mostly because it feels strange. We may not have seen our own fathers do it. Some men assume blessing is a priest's job. Others feel they are not holy enough to bless anyone. But the Church teaches that every baptized person is called to be a blessing and to bless. A father blessing his child is not overstepping. He is doing what fathers in the faith have always done.

It also does something for you. On a hard day, when there was a raised voice or a fight about homework, the bedtime blessing is a way to close the day with peace. It doesn't erase what happened. But it reminds both of you that the day does not have the last word. Love does.

Picture a night after a rough evening. Your son was sent to his room after a fight with his sister, and you said something sharper than you meant. At bedtime you stand in his doorway, unsure. In one version, you say goodnight from the hall and close the door, and the day ends cold. In another, you sit on the edge of his bed, put your thumb on his forehead, and say, God bless you, I love you. He doesn't answer. But his shoulders drop, and the day ends warm.

Here is what it can look like in an ordinary week. Monday, your daughter is tired and barely notices. Wednesday, your son flinches a little, unsure what you are doing. By Saturday, after a long day of visiting relatives, you forget, and halfway down the hall you hear a small voice call out asking whether you are going to bless her. Practices like this take root quietly. You may not see them grow until the night they are missed.

You can say different words on different nights. Sometimes a line from Scripture. Sometimes something specific to that child and that day. God bless your kind heart. May the Lord give you courage for tomorrow. The words matter less than the faithfulness.

The kids may think it is strange at first. That's fine. Keep doing it. Within a week or two, it becomes part of bedtime, and you may find they come looking for it.

What if you are not holy enough? None of us are. The blessing does not come from your goodness. It comes from God, and you are simply the one who passes it on. And what if an older child pulls away? Keep it brief, maybe just a hand on the shoulder and a quiet God bless you. Even teenagers who act indifferent often notice on the night you forget.

Christmas is the feast of the Father's blessing poured out on the world in his Son. Tonight, pass a little of that blessing on.

As you trace the cross, think about what you want to speak over their lives. Then start tonight, and keep doing it every night after.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is blessing each child at bedtime. A bedtime blessing is a short, old Christian practice. You place your thumb on your child's forehead, trace a small sign of the cross, and say a few words over them. It takes ten seconds. It works because it joins touch, attention, and faith in one small moment, and tells a child that he belongs to God and is loved by his father.

Here is how to do it. At bedtime, after prayers or after the lights go out, go to each child. Rest your hand on their head or cheek. Trace the cross on the forehead with your thumb. Then say one short line.

Here are some examples. God bless you, and keep you, and make you strong. May the Lord bless you and keep you. Or simply the child's name, followed by, In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. You can also speak something specific over them. God bless your kind heart. May the Lord give you courage tomorrow.

On a hard day, do not skip it. A blessing after a raised voice or a fight about homework is a way to close the day in peace. It does not erase what happened. It reminds both of you that love has the last word.

The kids may find it strange at first. Keep going anyway. Within a week or two it becomes part of bedtime, and they may start to ask for it. Start tonight, and keep doing it every night after.
days.fact: In Luke chapter 2, verse 34, when Mary and Joseph bring the infant Jesus to the Temple, the old man Simeon takes the child in his arms and praises God. Then Luke says Simeon blessed them, meaning the parents. Before Joseph and Mary carried their son home, they received a blessing themselves. Parents who bless their children need blessing too.

dailyVerse.text: The Lord bless you and keep you. The Lord make his face shine upon you and be gracious to you. The Lord look upon you kindly and give you peace.

days.church: The Church teaches that parents, above all others, are obliged to form their children in faith and Christian living by word and example. That is canon seven seventy-four of the Code of Canon Law. A nightly blessing is both. The words place your child in God's hands, and the sign of the cross shows him that his father belongs to Christ and wants him to belong to Christ too.

days.title: Repair the holiday
days.teach: Holidays create ruptures: too many people, too little sleep, too many expectations. Today is for quiet repair, rest, and leftovers. Make any apology you owe: specific, brief, no excuses. Then bring the routine back gently, one piece at a time. Don't let the holiday excuse old habits.
days.do: Repair anything from the last few days.
days.ask: Did I let the holiday excuse old habits?
days.talk:
This week's verse tells how the boy Jesus went down with Mary and Joseph to Nazareth after three anxious days in Jerusalem. A frightening rupture, and then a homecoming, and then ordinary life again. That pattern belongs to every family, and it belongs especially to the day after Christmas.

Christmas is over. The house is quieter, maybe messier, and you may be looking back over the last few days with some regret. Holidays create ruptures. Too many people, too little sleep, too much sugar, too many expectations. Somewhere in there, voices may have been raised. Maybe yours.

That is normal. It does not undo the progress you have made. But it does call for something. Today is for quiet repair, rest, and leftovers.

Why do good fathers skip repair after a holiday? Because everyone wants to move on. The tree is still up, the kids are playing with new toys, and bringing up a bad moment feels like spoiling the mood. There is pride in it too. It is hard to go back to a child and admit you were wrong. So we hope the moment simply fades. Sometimes it does fade from our memory. It rarely fades from theirs.

Start with any apology you owe. Be specific and brief. Something like, Yesterday I raised my voice when you were slow getting ready. That was wrong, and I'm sorry. No speech. No explaining why you were stressed. No asking them to apologize back. Just owning your part. When you repair cleanly, your child learns that a relationship can take a hit and recover. That lesson matters more than any perfect holiday.

Picture the car on the way home from a relative's house. Your daughter was dragging her feet leaving, and you snapped at her in front of everyone. The ride home was silent. In one version of the next morning, nobody mentions it, and she stays a little guarded with you for days without knowing why. In the other, you find her at the kitchen table, sit down, and say three honest sentences. She shrugs and says it's okay. Then she asks if you want to see the game she got. The door is open again.

Some fathers worry that apologizing to a child weakens their authority. It does the opposite. A father who can say I was wrong shows his children that his authority rests on something solid. He is not pretending to be perfect. He is showing them what a strong man does after a mistake. Children respect that, even when they cannot say so.

If your wife was on the receiving end of a sharp word over the holidays, she deserves a repair too. The same rules apply. Specific, brief, no excuses. Children notice when their father apologizes to their mother, and it teaches them as much as any apology made to them.

Then bring the routine back gently. You don't need to snap everything into place this morning. Bedtime moves back toward normal over the next few nights. The daily rhythm you drafted before the break comes back one piece at a time. A lazy day with leftovers and a movie is a fine start, as long as it heads back toward the structure the kids rely on.

The danger after a holiday is letting the holiday excuse old habits. It was Christmas, everyone was tired, so the yelling didn't count. But it did count, to your kids. Repair is how you close it out.

Think of Peter after the Resurrection. He had denied Jesus three times by a charcoal fire. Then, on the shore of Galilee, by another charcoal fire, Jesus asked him three times, Do you love me? Three denials, three chances to answer with love. Jesus did not pretend the betrayal had not happened. He repaired it, specifically and gently, and then he gave Peter his work again. That is the shape of good repair.

This week's Scripture shows the boy Jesus going home to Nazareth with his parents after a frightening few days in Jerusalem. The story ends with a family coming home together and returning to ordinary life. That is what today is for.

So look back honestly at the last few days. Was there anything that needs mending? Take care of it today, quietly and soon.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is repairing anything from the last few days. Repair is what you do after a rupture, a moment when you raised your voice, said something sharp, or treated a child unfairly. You go back, own your part, and reconnect. It works because a child who sees a relationship take a hit and recover learns that love is sturdier than a bad moment.

First, look back honestly over the holidays. Was there a moment you would rather take back? A raised voice in the kitchen, a sharp word in the car, a promise you broke?

Then go to that child, privately, and keep it short. Name what you did. Say it was wrong. Say you are sorry. For example. Yesterday I raised my voice when you were slow getting ready. That was wrong, and I'm sorry. Or. I snapped at you in front of your cousins. You didn't deserve that. I'm sorry. No speech about how stressed you were. No asking them to apologize back. Just your part. If your wife was on the receiving end of anything, she deserves a repair too.

Then reconnect. A hug, a few minutes together, an invitation to help with something.

Second, bring the routine back gently. Bedtime moves back toward normal over the next few nights. The break rhythm you drafted, the loose daily shape with a wake time, a job, outside time, and screens after, comes back one piece at a time. A lazy day with leftovers and a movie is a fine start, as long as tomorrow heads back toward structure.
days.fact: In Tobit chapter 11, the son Tobias returns home after his long travels. His mother Anna, who had watched the road for him, runs to embrace him. Then Tobias treats his blind father's eyes, and Tobit's sight returns. Tobit sees his son, throws his arms around his neck, and weeps. A family broken by distance and suffering is made whole again in a homecoming.

dailyVerse.text: Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ has forgiven you.

days.church: The Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraph twenty-two twenty-three, teaches that parents should give their children good example, and that by acknowledging their own failings to their children, they are better able to guide and correct them. A specific, brief apology after a hard holiday does not weaken your authority. It shows your children how a man of faith owns his mistakes and begins again.

days.title: The Holy Family
days.teach: Even the Holy Family had a crisis: a lost child, three days of searching, and a mother saying "your father and I have been searching for you anxiously" (Lk 2:48). Then Jesus "was obedient to them." Real families have hard days. Holiness is not avoiding them; it is coming home together.
days.do: Read Luke 2:41-52 aloud at dinner.
days.ask: What would it look like to search for my kids' hearts?
days.talk:
Today is the Feast of the Holy Family. It is easy to imagine that family as serene, with nothing ever going wrong. But Luke tells us otherwise.

Even the Holy Family had a crisis. On the way home from Jerusalem, Jesus was missing. Mary and Joseph spent three days searching for him. Imagine those three days. The fear. The retracing of every step. The sleepless nights. When they finally found him in the Temple, his mother said to him, your father and I have been searching for you anxiously.

There is something comforting in that. The holiest family in history had a hard day. Mary did not hide her distress. Joseph was right there with her, searching too. And Luke records that she named it out loud, to the boy, and to all of us.

Notice also how Jesus answered. Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house? And Luke adds that they did not understand what he said to them. Even Mary and Joseph did not fully understand their son. If there are days you cannot make sense of your own child, you are in holy company.

Why does this feast matter so much for a father trying to stop yelling? Because many of us carry a picture of the perfect family, the one on the Christmas card, and we measure our own house against it. Every argument becomes proof that we are failing. That picture makes us harder on ourselves and, often, harder on our kids. Luke gives us a truer picture.

Then comes the line that has been our verse all week. Jesus went down with them to Nazareth and was obedient to them. The crisis did not break the family. They went home together. Life resumed. He grew in wisdom and stature.

That is the shape of holiness in a real family. Not the absence of hard days, but coming home together after them. Real families have bad mornings, lost tempers, misunderstandings, and frightened nights. What makes a family holy is not avoiding all of that. It is returning to each other, again and again.

The Church calls the family a domestic church, a small church in the home. That does not mean a perfect home. It means a home where prayer, forgiveness, and ordinary love are practiced day after day. Nazareth was exactly that. Your house can be too, even on the days that feel far from holy.

There is something else here too. Mary and Joseph searched for their son. Think about what it would look like to search for your children's hearts. To pay attention when they seem far away. To go looking for them, instead of waiting for them to come back on their own.

Picture the dinner table tonight. In one version, you read the passage and then deliver a long lesson about obeying your parents, and the kids stare at their plates until it ends. In another, you read it slowly, ask how Mary and Joseph must have felt, and listen. Your youngest says he would have been scared. Your oldest says Jesus should have told them where he was. Everyone laughs. Then you say one sentence about how every family has hard days. That is all it needs.

Notice too that Joseph is silent in this story. Mary speaks for both of them, but he was there for all three days of searching. He did not need to make a speech to show his love. He showed it by looking, by staying, and by walking home beside his son afterward. Many fathers express love best this way, in faithful presence rather than words. That is a real gift, as long as the presence is warm and not distant.

And if one of your children seems far away right now, quieter than usual, spending more time behind a closed door, take that as your cue. Mary and Joseph did not wait in Jerusalem for their son to find them. They went looking. You can go looking too, with a walk, a drive, or an invitation to help you with something.

You may worry the kids will roll their eyes at a Bible reading at dinner. Some will, at first. Keep it short, keep it light, and don't turn it into a test. Children remember stories far longer than they remember lectures.

Tonight at dinner, read this story aloud from Luke's Gospel, chapter two, starting at verse forty one. Let the kids hear that the Holy Family had a hard day too, and that they came home together.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is reading the story of the boy Jesus lost in the Temple aloud at dinner. It is in Luke's Gospel, chapter two, starting at verse forty one and ending at verse fifty two. It takes about two minutes to read. It works because children are comforted to learn that the Holy Family had a hard day too, and that they came home together afterward.

Here is how to do it. Have a Bible or the passage on your phone ready before dinner, and keep the phone face down otherwise. Once everyone has started eating, tell them what you are about to read. For example. Today is the Feast of the Holy Family. I want to read you a story about a really hard day they had.

Read slowly. Let an older child read part of it if they like. Then ask one or two simple questions, and keep it light. How do you think Mary and Joseph felt when they couldn't find him? What would you do if you got lost in a crowd? Why do you think Luke wrote down that they went home together?

Then say one sentence about your own family. For example. Every family has hard days, even the holiest one. What matters is that we come back to each other. Leave it there. This is not a lecture.

Afterward, think about the question for today. What would it look like to search for your children's hearts? Which child seems far away right now? Go looking for that one this week, instead of waiting.
days.fact: In Luke chapter 2, verses 41 and 42, before the story of the boy Jesus lost in Jerusalem, Luke notes that Mary and Joseph went to Jerusalem every year for the feast of Passover. The pilgrimage when Jesus was twelve was not a one-time trip but part of a family habit. The Holy Family's life of faith had a yearly rhythm they kept together.

dailyVerse.text: When his parents saw him they were astonished, and his mother said, Son, why have you done this to us? Your father and I have been searching for you anxiously.

days.church: The Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraph five thirty-four, reflects on the finding of the boy Jesus in the Temple, and paragraph five thirty-two recalls that at Nazareth he was obedient to Mary and Joseph. Paragraphs sixteen fifty-six and sixteen fifty-seven call the family the domestic church, the first school of Christian life, where patience, forgiveness and prayer are learned. Holiness means coming home together after hard days.

days.focus: Day 90 is Jan 2. Day 91 (Epiphany, Jan 3): family meeting to celebrate and decide what stays.
days.verse: As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.
days.title: Read the data
days.teach: Count the X's on the wall chart. Compare yell counts and how often the kids followed the first request in week 1 versus now. Memory is a poor judge; numbers cut through good days and bad. Be honest. Improvement, not perfection, is the measure.
days.do: Total up the 90 days so far.
days.ask: What changed most? What changed least?
days.talk:
This is the final week, and our verse comes from Joshua. As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord. Before Joshua said those famous words, he did something important. He stood before the people and told them, one event after another, everything God had done for them. He looked back honestly before he looked ahead.

That is where we are now. Before you celebrate, it is time to look honestly at what has happened. Today is about reading the data.

Go to the wall chart and count the X's. Then compare. Look at your yell counts in week one and your yell counts now. Look at how often the kids followed the first request in week one versus now. Write the numbers down side by side.

This matters because memory is a poor judge. On a good day, you may feel like you've arrived. On a bad day, you may feel like nothing has changed at all. Numbers cut through both. They show you what actually happened, not what you remember feeling.

Why do so many fathers avoid this step? Because counting feels like a verdict. Some men fear the numbers will show they failed. Others are afraid the numbers will look good and they will get complacent. And some simply let the chart slide during the holidays and feel embarrassed to look at the gaps. All of that is understandable. None of it is a reason to skip the count.

It's the same reason good doctors track outcomes. A careful surgeon doesn't judge a procedure by how the last case felt. He looks at the results across many patients, honestly, including the ones that went poorly. That is how you learn what works.

So be honest. If the yell count dropped but didn't hit zero, write that down. If the kids follow first requests more often but still not always, write that down too. Improvement, not perfection, is the measure. A father who went from yelling most days to yelling once a week has changed something real in his home, even if the change isn't finished.

Picture a father at the kitchen table late at night with the chart in front of him. He is braced for bad news, because Christmas week was rough. Then he counts. Week one had a mark nearly every day, sometimes two or three. This week has two. He sits back in his chair. The rough week had felt like a collapse. The numbers say it was a dip on a line that has been heading in the right direction for months.

What if your records are patchy? Use what you have. Your notes, your calendar, and your wife's memory together will give you a rough picture, and a rough picture is enough. What if a number got worse? Then you have learned something valuable. Look at when it happens. Mornings, homework, the end of a long workday. That is not a failure. It is a map for where to focus next.

And bring your wife into this if you can. She has her own sense of how the house has changed, and her view may differ from yours. Put her impressions next to your numbers. Where they agree, you can be confident. Where they differ, you have something worth talking about together over coffee this week.

Then ask yourself two questions. What changed most? And what changed least? The first tells you what to keep doing. The second tells you where to focus next. Both are useful. Neither is a verdict on whether you are a good father.

Scripture gives us a picture of honest remembering. When the people of Israel finally crossed the Jordan into the promised land, Joshua had twelve men each carry a stone from the middle of the riverbed. They set the stones up as a memorial. When your children ask what these stones mean, Joshua said, you will tell them what the Lord did here. The stones were not for pride. They were for remembering accurately, so that the next generation would know the story.

This week we hear Joshua's words, As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord. Joshua said that after looking back over everything God had done for his people. Remembering comes before recommitting.

So today, take a few minutes, gather the charts, and total up the ninety days so far.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is totaling up the ninety days so far. This is a short, honest review of your records. It works because memory is a poor judge. A good day makes you think you have arrived, and a bad day makes you think nothing has changed. Numbers show what actually happened.

Start with the wall chart. That is the simple calendar or tracking sheet where you have been marking your days with an X and noting how often you yelled. If your records are patchy, use what you have, your notes, and your wife's memory. Rough numbers still tell the story.

Then make two columns on a sheet of paper, one for week one and one for this week. Write down two things in each.

First, your yell count. How many times did you raise your voice in week one? How many this week? For example. Eleven in week one. Three this week.

Second, first requests followed. That means how often the kids did what you asked the first time you asked, without repeating, reminding, or raising your voice. A rough estimate is fine. For example. About one in four back then. About two in three now.

Look at the two columns side by side. Then answer two questions in a sentence each. What changed most? What changed least? The first tells you what to keep doing. The second tells you where to focus in the new year.

Be honest. If the number went down but not to zero, write it down anyway. Improvement, not perfection, is the measure. Neither column is a verdict on whether you are a good father.
days.fact: In Luke chapter 2, verse 52, after Jesus returns to Nazareth with Mary and Joseph, Luke sums up his years there in one sentence. He grew in wisdom, in stature, and in favor with God and with people. That is four kinds of growth, of the mind, the body, the soul, and relationships, all happening in an ordinary home under his parents' care.

dailyVerse.text: Let us search and examine our ways, and return to the Lord.

days.church: The Church teaches that regular confession of everyday faults is strongly recommended, because it helps form our conscience and fight our evil tendencies. That is paragraph fourteen fifty-eight of the Catechism of the Catholic Church. Honest review is a Catholic habit. Counting what changed and what did not is a small examination of conscience for your fatherhood, and a good preparation for your next confession.

days.focus: Day 90 is Jan 2. Day 91 (Epiphany, Jan 3): family meeting to celebrate and decide what stays.
days.verse: As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.
days.title: Fade the points
days.teach: Once a behavior is steady, phase the points out gradually and keep the praise going. Retire one target at a time, and keep the chart only for targets that still need it. The goal was always habits, not a permanent reward system.
days.do: With your wife, pick which targets to retire.
days.ask: What still needs the chart?
days.talk:
Joshua told the people, As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord. Notice what kind of sentence that is. It is not a reward chart. It does not say we will serve the Lord as long as we earn something for it. It is a statement about who a family is. That is where these ninety days have been heading, and today you take one more step toward it.

Over these weeks, the points chart has done its job. It made expectations clear, gave the kids something to work toward, and helped turn good behavior into routine. But the chart was never meant to last forever.

Once a behavior is steady, you phase the points out gradually and keep the praise going. That is the key. Gradually. You don't tear the chart down tomorrow. You retire one target at a time, the ones that have become habits, and you keep the chart only for the targets that still need it.

Why gradually? Because a sudden stop can feel like the rules changed, and some kids will test whether the behavior still matters. A slow fade lets the habit carry the weight that the points used to carry.

Good fathers tend to make one of two mistakes here. Some hold on to the chart too long, because it works and they are afraid of what happens without it. Others drop it all at once, usually out of fatigue. The chart has been one more thing to track, and after the holidays nobody wants to update it. Both are understandable. A slow, deliberate fade avoids both.

And why keep the praise? Because praise is the part that was doing the deeper work all along. Points are a scaffold. Your attention and your words are the building. When you notice your son getting his shoes on without a reminder, or your daughter clearing her plate without being asked, and you say so, that still matters, chart or no chart.

Picture two homes in January. In the first, the chart quietly disappears from the fridge one weekend. No one says anything. By the next week, shoes are piling up by the door again, and a frustrated father is raising his voice about something that had been fixed for a month. In the second, the father tells his son at the Sunday meeting that he doesn't need points for shoes anymore, because it is a habit now. The boy stands a little taller. And every few days his father still notices out loud.

What if a behavior slips after you retire it? Then bring that one target back for a short while, with no shame and no speech. It just needed a little more scaffolding. What if your wife thinks a target is ready and you don't? Keep it on the chart a while longer. When in doubt, wait. And present the decision to the kids together, so they hear one plan.

Saint Paul wrote that when he was a child, he spoke like a child and thought like a child, but when he became a man, he put away childish things. He also told one young church that he had fed them with milk, because they were not yet ready for solid food. Growth means the supports change over time. Milk was right for a season. So was the chart. Taking it away slowly is not losing ground. It is a sign your children are growing.

When you retire a target, mark the moment. Tell the child specifically what changed and why you are proud of it. That turns the loss of points into a small graduation instead of a quiet disappearance.

The goal was always habits, not a permanent reward system. You want children who make their beds because that is what you do in this family, not because it earns three points. Fading the chart well is how you get there.

Joshua told the people, As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord. That is a statement about who a family is, not what it earns. That's where you're heading.

So sit down with your wife today. Look at the chart together and decide which targets are steady enough to retire, and which still need the chart a while longer. Make the decision together, so the kids hear one plan. Then make the first change this week.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is deciding with your wife which point chart targets to retire. A point chart is the simple chart where each child earns points or checkmarks for specific behaviors, called targets, like getting ready on time or doing homework before screens. It worked as a scaffold. Now the goal is to take it down slowly, so the habits stand on their own.

Sit down with your wife tonight and look at the chart together. Go through each target and sort it into one of two groups.

Retire it if the behavior has been steady for at least two weeks with little or no reminding. For example. Shoes and backpack by the door before breakfast. Clearing your plate after dinner.

Keep it if the behavior still slips, or if it is newer. For example. Starting homework without being asked. Getting into bed on time.

Then plan the fade. Retire only one or two targets this week, not all of them. Tell the kids at the family meeting, and frame it as a win. For example. You've gotten so good at getting ready in the mornings that you don't need points for it anymore. That's a habit now. You can also step down gradually first, giving points every other day before stopping altogether.

Most important, keep the praise going. Labeled praise means naming the exact thing you liked. For example. You got your shoes on without a reminder. That made our morning easy. Praise was doing the deeper work all along. Keep it coming long after the points are gone.
days.fact: In Sirach chapter 3, verse 5, the sage teaches that whoever honors his father will be gladdened by his own children, and when he prays he will be heard. Sirach pictures family faithfulness as something that passes forward. The way a man treats his own father shapes the joy he later finds in his children. Habits of honor, in this view, outlast a single generation.

dailyVerse.text: When I was a child, I spoke like a child, thought like a child, reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I put away childish things.

days.church: The Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraph twenty-three thirty-nine, teaches that self-mastery is a training in human freedom. The points chart was always a scaffold for that training. As a behavior becomes steady, letting the chart go invites your child to choose the good freely, because it has become his own habit, while your praise keeps encouraging him along the way.

days.focus: Day 90 is Jan 2. Day 91 (Epiphany, Jan 3): family meeting to celebrate and decide what stays.
days.verse: As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.
days.title: Your three non-negotiables
days.teach: Of everything you've practiced, which three will carry into 2027? Most fathers keep one-on-one time, the exit line, and the Sunday meeting. A short list gets kept; a long one gets forgotten by February. Pick the three that made the biggest difference in your house, and write them down. Ask what you would lose without each.
days.do: Write your three for 2027.
days.ask: What would I lose if I dropped these?
days.talk:
Joshua stood before the people and made a choice out loud. As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord. He did not give them a long list. He gave them one clear decision they could remember. That is the spirit of today.

You have practiced a lot of things over these ninety days. Pausing before reacting. The exit line. Repair. One on one time. Clear instructions. Praise. The Sunday meeting. Bedtime blessings. That is a lot to carry, and not all of it will survive the new year at full strength.

So here is the question. Of everything you have practiced, which three will carry into twenty twenty seven? Not ten. Three. The ones you will protect even when work gets busy and the kids get older and life gets in the way.

Why do good fathers struggle here? Because at the end of something meaningful, we feel enthusiastic. We want to keep everything. So we make a long list of resolutions, and it feels wonderful on the first of January. Then a hard week at work arrives, a child gets sick, the routine breaks, and the long list collapses all at once. When everything is a priority, nothing is.

Most fathers keep one on one time, the exit line, and the Sunday meeting. That makes sense. One on one time keeps the relationship strong with each child. The exit line keeps you from saying things you will regret. The Sunday meeting keeps you and your wife and the kids on the same page every week. But your three may be different. Pick the ones that have made the biggest difference in your house.

Why only three? Because a short list gets kept, and a long list gets forgotten. In the operating room, the safety checklist that works is the one short enough that people actually use it every time. A habit you keep beats a dozen you abandon by February.

Picture a Tuesday night in February. You come home late, tired, with a stack of work still on your mind. If you made a list of twelve resolutions, you will glance at it and feel guilty about the eleven you are not doing, and then you will do none of them. If you have three, you can look at the page on the closet door and think, I can still give my son fifteen minutes before bed. And you do.

Make each one concrete. Not be more patient, but use my exit line before my voice goes up. Not spend more time with the kids, but fifteen minutes with each child three nights a week. A vague promise is easy to break without noticing. A specific one tells you plainly whether you kept it.

Once you pick them, ask yourself what you would lose if you dropped each one. Picture the house without it. That is the reason you will keep it on the hard days.

What if your wife would choose a different three? Ask her. You may find you share one or two, and those are the strongest. You don't need identical lists. You need to know what each of you is protecting, so you can back each other up. And what about the practices that don't make your three? They are not forbidden. They just are not the ones you will fight for on a bad week.

Scripture is full of short lists that last. The prophet Micah asked what the Lord requires of us, and answered with three things. To do justice, to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God. When Jesus was asked for the greatest commandment, he gave two. Love God with all your heart, soul, and mind, and love your neighbor as yourself. God knows how human memory works. The most important things are often the shortest.

Joshua stood before the people and made a choice out loud. As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord. He did not leave it vague. He named it and committed to it in front of witnesses. Writing your three down is a small version of that.

So today, take a piece of paper and write your three for twenty twenty seven. Put it where you will see it.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is writing down your three non negotiables for twenty twenty seven. A non negotiable is a practice you will protect even when work is busy, the kids get older, and life gets in the way. It works because a short list gets kept, and a long list gets forgotten by February.

Start by listing everything you have practiced over these ninety days. Pausing before reacting. The exit line, the short sentence you say before you step away from rising anger. Repair, going back to own your part after a hard moment. One on one time with each child. Clear instructions. Labeled praise. The Sunday family meeting. The bedtime blessing.

Then pick three. Ask which ones made the biggest difference in your house. Many fathers choose these three. One on one time, because it keeps each relationship strong. The exit line, because it keeps you from saying things you will regret. The Sunday meeting, because it keeps the whole family on the same page every week. But yours may be different.

For each one, write it down in a single plain sentence with a when attached. For example. Fifteen minutes alone with each child, three nights a week. I use my exit line before my voice goes up. Family meeting every Sunday after dinner.

Then, next to each one, write what you would lose if you dropped it. That is your reason on the hard days.

Put the page somewhere you will see it every day. The bathroom mirror, the inside of your closet door, or the first page of your planner. Show it to your wife.
days.fact: Hebrews chapter 11 remembers fathers passing faith forward. In verses 20 and 21, Isaac blesses Jacob and Esau about things to come, and the dying Jacob blesses each of Joseph's sons while worshiping as he leans on the top of his staff. Verse 23 credits Moses' parents for hiding him. Then chapter 12 opens by calling all these people a great cloud of witnesses surrounding us as we run.

dailyVerse.text: He has shown you what is good. What does the Lord require of you but to do justice, to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?

days.church: The Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraph twenty-one eighty-six, teaches that Sunday is a day to give time and care to family, and to rest. As you choose your three practices for the new year, build them around the Lord's Day. Sunday Mass, a family meeting, and unhurried time together can anchor the whole week, even when work grows heavy.

days.focus: Day 90 is Jan 2. Day 91 (Epiphany, Jan 3): family meeting to celebrate and decide what stays.
days.verse: As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.
days.title: A letter to each child
days.teach: Write each child a short letter: what you see in them, what you're proud of, and what you've learned as their father these 90 days. Be specific. Give it to them, or seal it for a milestone. Written words can be read again and again.
days.do: Write a letter to each child.
days.ask: What do I want them to know if they never hear it otherwise?
days.talk:
Near the end of his long speech, after the people promised to serve the Lord, the book of Joshua tells us that Joshua wrote these words in the book of the law of God. He did not trust the moment to memory alone. He wrote it down. Today, on the last day of the year, you have a writing assignment too. Write each of your children a short letter.

Not a long one. A page is plenty. Tell them three things. What you see in them. What you are proud of. And what you have learned as their father over these ninety days.

Why does this matter so much? Because most fathers love their children far more than they ever say. We assume our kids know. We show love by working, driving, providing, and fixing things, and we trust that the message gets through. Often it does. But children also need to hear it in words, and many men find those words hard to say out loud. Some of us never heard them from our own fathers, so we have no model for how they sound. A letter gives you time to find them.

What you see in them means the good qualities you notice. His curiosity. Her courage on a hard first day. The kindness one of them showed a younger child. Be specific. Children believe specific praise much more than general compliments.

What you are proud of means not just achievements, but effort and character. The time he kept going when something was hard. The way she handled a disappointment at a game or a recital.

And what you have learned as their father. This is the part that may surprise them. A father admitting he has been learning tells a child that growth is something grown ups do too. You might write that you learned to slow down, or to listen better, or that you are sorry for times you yelled and grateful they gave you another chance.

Picture a young woman, years from now, on the night before she leaves home. She is packing, nervous, unsure of herself. In a drawer she finds a folded page in her father's handwriting. It tells her she is brave, that he saw it on a hard first day at a new school, and that he is proud of the way she treats people. She reads it twice and puts it in her suitcase. Spoken words from that winter have long since faded. These are still there.

Write a different letter for each child. Do not copy one into the others. Children compare, and each one should be able to tell that the letter was written only for them. If you have several children, that may take more than one sitting. That is fine. Write one today and the others this week if you need to. What matters is that each child receives a letter that could not belong to anyone else.

Then decide what to do with it. You can give it to them now. Or you can seal it and keep it for a milestone, a confirmation, a graduation, a hard day years from now when they need to know what their father thought of them.

Some fathers say they are not writers. You don't need to be. Plain words in your own handwriting are worth more than polished ones. Write the way you talk. Others worry the letter will embarrass an older child. Then seal it for later. A teenager who would squirm today may treasure it at twenty five.

Scripture holds many letters from a spiritual father to his children. Saint Paul wrote to Timothy and opened with the words, To Timothy, my beloved child. Paul could not always be with the people he loved, so he wrote to them, and the Church has been reading those letters for two thousand years. A father's written words can outlast him in ways he never imagines.

Here is the question to hold while you write. What do you want them to know if they never hear it otherwise? Words spoken aloud fade. Words written down can be read again and again.

Joshua told the people that he and his house would serve the Lord, and he wrote those words in the book of the law. Some commitments deserve to be written down. So does a father's love.

Find a quiet hour today, and write each letter.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is writing a short letter to each of your children. One page is plenty. It works because spoken words fade, but a letter can be read again and again, sometimes years later, on the day a child most needs to know what his father thought of him.

Find a quiet hour. Write by hand if you can. Give each letter three parts.

First, what you see in them. Name specific qualities, with a real example. For example. You are curious. I love the way you take things apart to see how they work.

Second, what you are proud of. Focus on effort and character, not only results. For example. I'm proud of how you kept going at practice when it was hard. Or. I'm proud of how kindly you treated your little cousin at Christmas.

Third, what you have learned as their father. This is the part that may surprise them. For example. These last few months I've been learning to slow down and listen better. I'm sorry for the times I yelled. Thank you for giving me another chance.

Close with something simple. I love you, and I'm proud to be your dad.

Write a different letter for each child. Do not copy one into the others. Each child should be able to tell it was written only for them.

Then decide what to do with each one. Give it to them now, perhaps at the celebration meeting. Or seal it and keep it for a milestone, like a confirmation or a graduation. Either way, ask yourself what they need to know if they never hear it otherwise. Write that.
days.fact: In Luke chapter 1, verses 62 to 64, when John the Baptist is born, the relatives assume he will be named after his father. Zechariah, who has been unable to speak for months, asks for a writing tablet and writes that his name is John. Immediately his mouth is opened and he begins to praise God. A father's first words for his son were written ones.

dailyVerse.text: To Timothy, my beloved child: grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.

days.church: The Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraph twenty-two thirty-two, teaches that family ties are important but not absolute. Each child has a vocation of his own, a path God is calling him to walk. A letter that names what you see in your child honors that calling. It tells him his father noticed the person God is making, and it can travel with him long after he leaves home.

days.focus: Day 90 is Jan 2. Day 91 (Epiphany, Jan 3): family meeting to celebrate and decide what stays.
days.verse: As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.
days.title: Mary, Mother of God
days.teach: New Year's Day. Mary "kept all these things, pondering them in her heart." Sit with your wife today and look back on these 90 days together. Ask what has changed, and what it has done for your marriage. Plan the next season, starting with date nights.
days.do: A look-back conversation with your wife.
days.ask: What has this done for our marriage?
days.talk:
Happy New Year. Today the Church celebrates Mary, the Mother of God. And in the Gospel for this feast, there is a quiet line about her. Mary kept all these things, pondering them in her heart.

She didn't rush past what had happened. Shepherds had come with a story about angels. Her newborn son lay in a manger. Everything was strange and holy and overwhelming. And Mary held it. She kept it. She turned it over in her heart and let its meaning settle.

That is what today is for. Sit with your wife and look back on these ninety days together. Not as a report or a performance review. As two people who have been through something together, pondering what it has meant.

Here is why this matters. When parenting gets hard, many couples slip into running the house like business partners. Who is driving which child where. Who handles the dentist. Who signs the permission slip. That kind of coordination is necessary. But if it is the only way you talk, the marriage slowly shrinks to logistics. Good husbands drift into this without ever choosing it, simply because the urgent things crowd out the important ones.

Ask each other questions. What has changed in the house? What has been hardest? What surprised you? When did you see the kids respond differently? When did you feel most like a team? Let her tell you what she has noticed, in you and in the children. She has had a front row seat.

And ask the question underneath it all. What has this done for our marriage? Ninety days of working on calm authority is not only about the kids. It has asked you and your wife to agree, to back each other up, to talk on Sundays, to repair with each other too. That is marriage work. It is worth naming.

Picture two versions of this conversation. In the first, you sit down, and within ten minutes you are discussing the school calendar and whose turn it is to call the plumber. In the second, you set the logistics aside on purpose. You ask her when she felt most proud of you this fall, and you listen. She tells you about an evening you walked out of the kitchen instead of shouting. You had forgotten it. She hadn't.

What if you and your wife remember these months differently? Let her version stand alongside yours. You are not trying to agree on a single record. You are trying to understand each other. And what if date nights feel impossible, with no babysitter and no budget? A walk around the neighborhood after the kids are in bed counts. So does coffee at the kitchen table before anyone else is awake.

Close by thanking her. Be specific about one thing she did over these months that made a difference. Maybe it was backing you up in front of the kids when you were not sure of yourself. Maybe it was a word of encouragement after a bad night. Thank her for that one thing. A wife who is thanked specifically knows she has been seen, and that matters to her as much as it matters to your children.

And if the conversation turns hard, if she names something that still hurts, do not defend yourself. Listen, thank her for telling you, and let it be part of the plan for the next season.

Then look ahead. Plan the next season together, and start with date nights. A strong marriage is the foundation of a calm home. Kids feel safest when they see their parents enjoying each other. Put the first few on the calendar today.

Think of Mary at the wedding at Cana. In the middle of a celebration, she noticed what others missed. The wine had run out. She paid attention to what a young couple needed. Today, pay that same kind of attention to your own marriage. Saint Paul told husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the Church. That love is not only shown in big sacrifices. It is shown in listening, noticing, and making time.

Joshua's words this week were As for me and my house. A house is built by two people who choose the same direction. Mary pondered. Today, you and your wife can ponder together.

Find a quiet stretch of time today for that look back conversation.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is a look back conversation with your wife. This is an unhurried talk, just the two of you, about what these ninety days have meant for your family and your marriage. It is not a performance review. It works because naming what you have been through together makes it shared, and planning the next season keeps it going.

Find forty five minutes when the kids are busy or asleep. Put your phones away. Sit somewhere comfortable, maybe with coffee or a glass of wine.

Take turns with questions like these. What has changed in the house? What has been hardest? When did you see the kids respond differently? When did we feel most like a team? What surprised you? Let her answer fully, and listen more than you talk. She has had a front row seat, and she may have seen things in you that you missed.

Then ask the question underneath. What has this done for our marriage? Agreeing on rules, backing each other up, talking on Sundays, and repairing with each other is marriage work too.

Then look ahead, starting with date nights. A date night is regular time for just the two of you, away from the kids and the logistics. Get your calendars out right now and put the first few on them. For example. Dinner out the second Friday of each month. A walk together every Saturday morning. Coffee alone after Sunday Mass.

Close by thanking her for walking beside you. Be specific about one thing she did. Then, like Mary, keep it and ponder it.
days.fact: In Second Timothy chapter 1, verse 5, Paul reminds Timothy that his sincere faith lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice. Acts chapter 16, verse 1 adds that Timothy's father was a Greek. Paul credits the women of Timothy's family with handing on the faith that made him a leader. Scripture honors faith passed down through mothers and grandmothers.

dailyVerse.text: But Mary treasured all these things, keeping them and pondering them in her heart.

days.church: The Church teaches that Mary is truly the Mother of God, because the son she bore is the eternal Son of God made man. The Catechism of the Catholic Church affirms this in paragraph four ninety-five, recalling the Council of Ephesus. Paragraph sixteen forty-one adds that spouses receive a proper grace of the sacrament to help each other. Today, ponder that grace together with your wife.

days.focus: Day 90 is Jan 2. Day 91 (Epiphany, Jan 3): family meeting to celebrate and decide what stays.
days.verse: As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.
days.title: Day 90
days.teach: You started because the house felt out of control. Look at who you've become: a father who exits instead of exploding, repairs instead of defending, and leads with warmth and structure. Habits drift slowly. Set a monthly check-in so they don't.
days.do: Put a monthly review on the calendar for 2027.
days.ask: What kind of father am I becoming?
days.talk:
Day ninety. You made it.

Joshua stood before the people at the end of a long road and said, As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord. Those words came at the end of a great deal of history, wandering and battles and mistakes and mercy. But they were not an ending. They were a promise about every day still to come. That is where you stand this morning.

Think back to where you started. You began this because the house felt out of control. Mornings were tense. Small things turned into shouting. You knew something had to change, and you suspected it had to start with you.

Now look at who you have become. A father who exits instead of exploding. A father who repairs instead of defending. A father who leads with warmth and structure. You are not perfect. No father is. But you are different from the man who started this in October, and your children know it, even if they couldn't put it into words.

That change didn't come from a single breakthrough. It came from small, daily choices. Pausing. Walking out of the room. Coming back to apologize. Giving five focused minutes. Holding a limit calmly. Hundreds of small choices, made one day at a time.

But here is the honest truth. Habits drift. Not all at once, but slowly. A busy month at work, a hard stretch with one of the kids, a few short nights, and old patterns creep back. That is not failure. It is how people work. The answer is to check in on purpose before the drift becomes a slide.

Why does drift happen to good men? Because the thing that kept you focused these ninety days was a daily prompt. Every morning brought a new idea and a new assignment. Tomorrow that prompt is gone. Attention naturally moves on to whatever is loudest, a project, a problem, a deadline. And the old habit of yelling did not disappear. It is still there, waiting for a tired evening. Knowing that is not discouraging. It is simply realistic.

Picture a Thursday in March. Work has been heavy for weeks. You notice that you have raised your voice three evenings in a row, and you cannot quite remember when your last one on one time was. In one version of the story, nobody notices, and by summer the house sounds like it did in September. In the other, your monthly review comes up on the calendar that Sunday. You sit down, read your questions, and see the slide clearly. You go back to the basics that week. Sleep. Your exit line. Five focused minutes. Within days, the house is calmer again.

What if you fall back completely one day? Then remember that you know the way back now. You have walked it once. The Church gives us confession precisely because falling is human, and returning is always possible. A father who stumbles and returns is not a failure. He is a father who is still in the work.

Invite your wife into the review if she is willing. Two people notice more than one, and drift is often easier to see from across the room.

So set a monthly check in for the year ahead. One time each month to look at how it's going. Are you still doing your three non negotiables? Has the yelling crept back? What needs attention? It might take twenty minutes. It will keep what you have built.

Scripture tells how God fed Israel in the desert with manna. Each morning there was enough for that day, and the people were told not to store it up for the next. Whatever they tried to hoard spoiled. They had to gather it again every morning. Grace for fathers often works the same way. You cannot stock up on patience for the year. You receive it day by day, which is why Jesus taught us to pray for our daily bread.

Joshua made his promise for his whole house, and then he had to live it out year after year. So will you. The commitment is made once. The keeping of it is daily.

So ask yourself what kind of father you are becoming. Then open your calendar and put a monthly review on it for all of twenty twenty seven.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is putting a monthly review on your calendar for all of twenty twenty seven. A monthly review is a twenty minute check in with yourself, and ideally with your wife, to see whether the habits you built are still holding. It works because habits drift slowly, and a regular look catches the drift before it becomes a slide.

Open your calendar now. Pick a recurring time that will actually work. For example. The first Sunday evening of every month, after the kids are in bed. Set it to repeat all year, and add a reminder the day before.

Then write a short list of review questions and attach it to the calendar entry, so you are not starting from scratch each month. Keep it to four or five. For example. Am I still keeping my three non negotiables? Has the yelling crept back, and when does it happen? Am I still giving each child one on one time? Are we still holding the Sunday family meeting? What needs attention this month?

At each review, pick one thing to adjust, not five. If the yelling is creeping back, go back to the basics. Your exit line, the short sentence you say before you step away from rising anger. Sleep. Morning prayer.

If your wife is willing, do the review together. Two people notice more than one.

Before you close the calendar, ask yourself the question for today. What kind of father am I becoming? Write one sentence of answer in the first review entry. Next month, read it back.
days.fact: Malachi chapter 4, verse 6, numbered chapter 3 in some Bibles, promises that God will turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers. In most modern Bibles it is the last verse of the Old Testament. In Luke chapter 1, verse 17, the angel tells Zechariah that his son John will do exactly this.

dailyVerse.text: The steadfast love of the Lord never ceases, and his mercies never come to an end. They are new every morning; great is your faithfulness.

days.church: The Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraph two thirty-nine, teaches that calling God Father speaks of his authority and also of his goodness and loving care. God's fatherhood is the standard by which every human father is measured. No father reaches it in ninety days. But the measure stays the same, and a monthly look at your habits keeps you walking toward it.

days.focus: Day 90 is Jan 2. Day 91 (Epiphany, Jan 3): family meeting to celebrate and decide what stays.
days.verse: As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.
days.title: Epiphany: celebrate
days.teach: The Magi came, offered their gifts, and went home by another way. Your house has found a new way home too. Hold a celebratory family meeting: what changed, what the kids noticed, what stays. Thank them for their patience and forgiveness, and thank God.
days.do: Celebration family meeting. Let the kids pick the dessert.
days.ask: What new way home have we found?
days.talk:
Today is the Epiphany. The Magi followed the star, found the child with Mary his mother, knelt, and offered their gifts. Then, warned in a dream, they went home by another way.

That last detail is worth sitting with. They came one way and left another. Something had happened in that house that changed their route home. They could not go back the way they came.

Matthew also tells us how the Magi felt when the star stopped over the place where the child was. They rejoiced with exceedingly great joy. After a long road, uncertain and far from home, they let themselves celebrate. Joy was the right response to what God had done.

That is what these ninety days have been. You came into this program one way. You are leaving another. The house has found a new way home, and today is the day to celebrate it together.

Why is celebrating so hard for many fathers? Because we are built to look for the next problem. The moment one thing is fixed, our attention moves to whatever is still broken. That instinct helps at work. At home, it can mean children never hear that their effort mattered. They worked through these months too. They adjusted to new routines, new charts, and a father who was learning. They deserve to see the progress named and enjoyed.

So hold a celebratory family meeting. Not a review, not a lecture. A celebration. Talk about what changed. Ask the kids what they noticed. You may be surprised by what they say. Children often notice things adults miss, like the fact that Dad doesn't yell in the mornings anymore, or that bedtime feels different, or that they like their time alone with you.

Picture the evening going wrong. The meeting starts warm, but within a few minutes you slip into a list of everything that still needs work. Homework habits. Messy rooms. The kids go quiet, and the dessert sits untouched. Now picture it going right. You open by saying the family has been working hard and tonight is a party. Your youngest says mornings are better now. Your oldest says she likes it when you take her for drives. You write both down, and you smile, and you leave the rest for another Sunday.

What if a child says something hard, like remembering a time you yelled? Receive it. Thank them for telling you. It is a sign they feel safe enough to say it. What if one child is sullen and won't join in? Let it be. Not every child shows joy the same way, and an invitation still counts even when it is quietly declined.

Before the meeting, take a few minutes to prepare. Think of one specific thing about each child that you want to name tonight. Not a general compliment, but something you saw. The morning he got ready without a single reminder. The night she forgave you quickly after you lost your temper. Children light up when a father remembers details, because details prove he was paying attention all along.

And think about how you will open. A short, warm sentence is enough. We have been working on making our home calmer for ninety days, and tonight we are celebrating. That sets the tone, and it tells everyone at the table that this evening is about gratitude, not about grades or scores.

Then decide together what stays. Share your three non negotiables. Ask them what they want to keep. A routine they like. A special time. The Sunday meeting. When kids have a voice in what stays, they own it.

And thank them. Thank them for their patience while you were learning. Thank them for the times they forgave you. Thank them for trying new things too. A father who thanks his children teaches them more about humility and love than a hundred lessons could.

This is also a good moment to look ahead with hope rather than fear. The program ends today, but your fatherhood does not. There will be hard mornings again. There will be days you raise your voice. But your children now know what a calm house feels like, and so do you.

Then thank God. For the grace of these ninety days. For a wife who walked beside you. For children who are growing every day.

Joshua said it plainly. As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord. Today, your house can say it together.

And one last thing. Let the kids pick the dessert. Celebrations should taste good.
days.assign:
Your one thing today is the celebration family meeting. A family meeting is a short, regular gathering where everyone sits together, talks, and plans. Today's is different. It is a party, not a review, and the kids pick the dessert. It works because children own what they help choose, and a family that celebrates its progress together is more likely to keep it.

Let the kids choose the dessert ahead of time. Gather everyone after dinner, at the table or in the living room. Keep it to twenty or thirty minutes, and keep it warm.

Open with a short line. For example. We've been working on making our home calmer for ninety days. Tonight we're celebrating.

Then move through four parts.

First, what changed. Share one or two things you noticed.

Second, ask the kids what they noticed. For example. What's different at home since the fall? What do you like better now? Listen without correcting. Children often notice things adults miss.

Third, decide together what stays. Share your three non negotiables. Then ask each child what they want to keep. A routine they like. Special time with you. The Sunday meeting. Write their answers down.

Fourth, thank them. Thank them for their patience while you were learning, for forgiving you, and for trying new things too. Be specific with each child.

Close with a short prayer of thanks for the grace of these ninety days, for your wife, and for each child by name. If you like, end with Joshua's words together. As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.

Then serve the dessert.
days.fact: In Matthew chapter 2, verse 11, the Magi enter the house, not a stable, and find the child with Mary his mother. They bring three gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh. Matthew never says how many Magi there were. The tradition of three comes from the gifts. In verse 12, warned in a dream, they return home by another road.

dailyVerse.text: When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy. Entering the house, they saw the child with Mary his mother, and they fell down and worshiped him.

days.church: The Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraph five twenty-eight, teaches that the Epiphany shows Jesus as the Messiah of Israel, the Son of God and the Savior of the world. In the Magi, the nations come to worship him. They came seeking, found the child with Mary his mother, and went home changed. Thank God tonight for the ways your own house has been changed.
